# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Panel (AI SaaS Platform)

**Panel's document-analysis AI system puts it squarely inside the EU AI Act as a provider, with baseline GDPR and product-liability obligations layered on top — no gatekeeper, platform, or sector-specific regime (DMA, DSA, NIS2, CRA, DORA, MiCA) currently reaches a B2B enterprise API of this kind.**

## Bottom line
- AI Act is Prio 1: Panel is a confirmed AI system provider under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and the specific conformity-assessment burden hinges on whether its document-analysis outputs feed Annex III high-risk use cases (e.g., employment or credit decisions) — this determination is unresolved and drives the compliance roadmap.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI Act (Reg. 2024/1689) | 1 | **In Scope** | Panel's stated role is AI system provider; the Regulation governs "the development, placement on the market and use of products and services embedding AI technology" to establish harmonised rules on the development, placement on the market and use of products and services embedding AI technology or stand-alone AI applications in the Union[1]. If Panel's document-analysis engine incorporates a third-party foundation model, value-chain cooperation duties on model suppliers and integrators also attach. |
| GDPR (Reg. 2016/679) | 2 | **In Scope** | Panel processes personal data within customer documents as a B2B processor/controller; standard accountability, DPIA, and cross-border enforcement cooperation rules apply as routine hygiene, not an existential risk. |
| Product Liability Directive (Dir. 2024/2853) | 2 | **In Scope** | The Directive treats software providers as manufacturers for no-fault liability purposes: A developer or producer of software, including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council, should be treated as a manufacturer.[2] Panel's AI system is squarely captured. |

The AI Act is the one file that determines Panel's actual compliance workload for the next two years. The Regulation created an AI Office to police the highest-risk tier of obligations, and a pending Commission proposal would widen that office's reach: sectoral authorities continue to remain responsible for the supervision of AI systems related to products covered by that Union harmonisation legislation, Article 75(1) Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 should be modified to bring all AI systems based on general-purpose AI models developed by the same provider within the scope of the AI Office's supervision.[3] That signals tightening, not loosening, enforcement architecture even as simplification debates continue elsewhere. Separately, if Panel's document-analysis pipeline incorporates externally sourced models or components, the value-chain provisions matter directly: all relevant third parties, in particular those that are involved in the development, sale and the commercial supply of software tools, components, pre-trained models or data incorporated into the AI system, or providers of network services, should… make available the required information, training or expertise and cooperate, as appropriate, with providers to enable their control over all compliance relevant aspects of the AI system that falls under this Regulation.[4] Confirming Annex III exposure and mapping every upstream model supplier's disclosure obligations are the two concrete workstreams that resolve the Monitor-adjacent uncertainty into a fixed compliance plan.

## Political landscape & strategic play

The AI Office, housed within the Commission's DG CNECT, is the working-level body that will decide how document-analysis use cases are classified and how GPAI-based systems are supervised; the pending amendment proposal explicitly recasts its mandate to cover the role of the AI Office in monitoring and supervising compliance of such AI systems with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, while excluding AI systems related to products covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I to that Regulation[3]. On the data-protection side, national DPAs (in Germany, the federal and state authorities) enforce GDPR under EDPB coordination, which issues guidance to keep supervisory practice consistent across cross-border processing cases.

**Lobbying focus:** the highest-value venue is the AI Office's ongoing guidance and Code-of-Practice process for GPAI-based systems and Annex III classification criteria. A medium-sized B2B provider's realistic ask is participation in the Commission's stakeholder consultation rounds on high-risk classification guidance for enterprise document-processing use cases, not a formal complaint — Panel has no standing to escalate against a named incumbent, since none is identified in its profile.

**Coalitions:** the retrieved sources name no trade association, complainant group, or peer company already organized around Panel's specific AI Act or product-liability exposure, and Panel's own profile names no competitor — this is a genuine gap to fill through direct engagement rather than joining an existing bloc.

**Watchlist:**
- AI Office supervisory-scope amendment (proposal 2025/0500 family, doc 52025PC0836) — determines whether GPAI-based systems Panel deploys fall under central AI Office oversight rather than national market surveillance.
- National transposition of the Product Liability Directive (2024/2853) into German civil law — confirm implementing-statute status and effective date.
- AI value-chain disclosure practice under Article-level cooperation duties (doc 52023AP0236) — confirm which upstream model suppliers Panel relies on and their disclosure posture.
- Continued AI Office guidance on Annex III high-risk classification — the single fact that reclassifies Panel's entire AI Act workload if document-analysis outputs feed employment, credit, or similarly listed decisions.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|
| DMA (Reg. 2022/1925) | Not a gatekeeper; it is only when a core platform service constitutes an important gateway and is operated by an undertaking with a significant impact in the internal market and an entrenched and durable position… that such concerns arise[5] — Panel meets none of these criteria. | Designation as a gatekeeper core platform service. |
| DSA (Reg. 2022/2065) | Panel is a B2B processing service, not an intermediary hosting third-party content for the public. | Launching a public-facing hosting or marketplace function. |
| NIS2 (Dir. 2022/2555) | Panel's document-analysis API doesn't match the Directive's digital-provider categories (cloud, data centre, CDN, marketplace, search engine, social platform). | Operating as a designated cloud or managed-service provider under Annex I/II. |
| CRA (Reg. 2024/2847) | Panel supplies a remotely delivered SaaS API, not a "product with digital elements" placed on the market as hardware or shrink-wrapped software. | Distributing a downloadable or embedded software product. |
| Data Act (Reg. 2023/2854) | Targets connected/IoT product data holders sectors characterised by the concentration of a small number of manufacturers supplying connected products to end users[6] — Panel makes no connected product. | Selling a connected hardware device alongside the API. |
| DGA (Reg. 2022/868) | Panel is not a data-intermediation service or data-altruism organisation. | Operating a data-sharing intermediary service. |
| DORA (Reg. 2022/2554) | Panel is not a financial entity subject to ICT risk-management rules. | Becoming a designated critical ICT third-party provider to financial entities. |
| MiCA (Reg. 2023/1114) | No crypto-asset issuance or service activity of any kind. | Launching a crypto-asset or wallet product. |
| P2B (Reg. 2019/1150) | P2B governs consumer-facing intermediation services; Panel's customer base is exclusively B2B enterprise. | Operating a marketplace connecting third-party sellers to consumers. |
| eIDAS2 (Reg. 2024/1183) | Panel is not a wallet provider or relying party under the Digital Identity Framework. | Integrating EU Digital Identity Wallet issuance or acceptance. |
| EMFA (Reg. 2024/1083) | Panel is not a media service provider or video-sharing platform. | Entering media distribution or content curation. |
| ePrivacy Directive (Dir. 2002/58) | Core obligations target providers of publicly available electronic communications services and consumer tracking, not an enterprise B2B API. | Offering consumer-facing communications or tracking-based services. |
| Machinery Reg./Dir. (2023/1230, 2006/42) | Panel produces software only, not physical machinery. | Bundling the AI system with physical robotic or industrial equipment. |
| Consumer Rights Directive (2011/83) | B2C-only regime; Panel sells exclusively to enterprise customers. | Launching a direct-to-consumer product line. |
| Package Travel Directive (2015/2302) | No travel or package-organizing activity. | N/A — unrelated business model. |
| Web Accessibility Directive (2016/2102) | Applies to public-sector body websites/apps, not a private B2B vendor. | Becoming a public-sector body or contracted public digital service. |
| European Accessibility Act (2019/882) | Covers listed consumer products/terminal equipment; Panel's enterprise API isn't among them. | Selling consumer-facing terminals or e-reader style products. |
| Cybersecurity Act (Reg. 2019/881) | Establishes voluntary ICT certification schemes, not a mandatory obligation for Panel's product category today. | A future mandatory certification scheme naming SaaS AI APIs. |
| European Business Wallets (Proposal 2025/0838) | Still a Commission proposal, not adopted law. | Adoption and a mandate to support business-credential exchange. |
| Digital Services Tax proposals (2018/0147, 2018/0148) | Proposals never adopted into binding EU law. | Formal re-adoption and entry into force. |

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Industrial IoT Manufacturer (Connected Sensors & Controllers)

**The Cyber Resilience Act is now the company's binding compliance centre of gravity as a manufacturer of products with digital elements, with the Machinery Directive, NIS2 and the Data Act layered on top as bounded but real obligations — no AI Act, GDPR, DMA or DSA exposure exists given the no-AI, no-personal-data, B2B profile.**

## Bottom line

- CRA compliance (vulnerability handling, conformity assessment, technical documentation) is Prio 1 because connected sensors and controllers are squarely "products with digital elements" under a regime already in force with active ENISA/CSIRT enforcement infrastructure — this is not a future file, it is live obligation-building work now.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cyber Resilience Act (32024R2847) | 1 | **In Scope** | Connected sensors/controllers are products with digital elements; the Regulation requires manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and work with CSIRTs designated as coordinators, which provide helpdesk support in relation to the reporting obligations to manufacturers[1], alongside conformity documentation and, where used, authorised-representative mandates. |
| Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC (33006L0042) | 2 | **In Scope** | The Directive's definition of "manufacturer" means any natural or legal person who designs and/or manufactures machinery or partly completed machinery covered by this Directive and is responsible for the conformity of the machinery or the partly completed machinery"[2] covers controllers and safety-relevant components for factory automation; the Directive remains the binding text now. Its successor, the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, applies only from 20 January 2027 — plan the transition, do not treat it as current law yet. |
| NIS2 Directive (32022L2555) | 2 | **In Scope** | The Directive's sector annex names manufacture of computer, electronic and optical products, manufacture of electrical equipment, and manufacture of machinery and equipment n.e.c.[3] as covered activities, and the company's large size places it above the important-entity threshold. |
| Data Act (32023R2854) | 2 | **In Scope** | As a large manufacturer of connected products, none of the Data Act's microenterprise/small-enterprise design-obligation carve-outs apply — those exemptions and the one-year transitional period are reserved for enterprises that qualify as micro, small, or newly-medium given the current state of technology, it would be overly burdensome on microenterprises and small enterprises to impose further design obligations... A transitional period should apply to an enterprise that has qualified as a medium-sized enterprise for less than one year[4] — full data-access and sharing obligations apply from day one. |
| Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU | 2 | **Monitor** | Hinges on whether the connected sensors/controllers incorporate radio transmission (vs. wired fieldbus only) — confirm product-line radio functionality before scoping conformity assessment. |
| EU Cybersecurity Act (32019R0881) | 3 | **Monitor** | Certification is currently voluntary, but connected and automated cars, electronic medical devices, industrial automation control systems and smart grids are only some examples of sectors in which certification is already widely used or is likely to be used in the near future[5], and Member States retain power to make schemes mandatory nationally. |

The Cyber Resilience Act deserves the most attention because it is a fully binding Regulation with an operating enforcement chain, not a proposal. ENISA maintains the coordinated vulnerability database and works directly with manufacturers on disclosure, while national CSIRTs are tasked with helpdesk support specifically aimed at smaller suppliers, signalling the Commission expects broad manufacturer coverage rather than a narrow niche regime. The obligations attach to the product category — connected devices with digital elements — not to company size beyond the microenterprise carve-outs the Act does not extend to a large manufacturer. Treat this as the anchor compliance file for 2025-2026 procurement, engineering and legal workstreams alike.

## Political landscape & strategic play

Cybersecurity and product-safety rulemaking for connected industrial equipment sits across two Commission services: DG CNECT drives CRA implementation and delegated acts, while DG GROW owns the Machinery Regulation transition and Radio Equipment Directive enforcement. National market surveillance authorities and CSIRTs designated as coordinators under the CRA are the operational contact points a manufacturer will actually deal with on vulnerability reporting, not Brussels-level political actors. On standardisation, the European Standardisation Organisations are actively drafting the harmonised standards that will carry presumption of conformity for IoT and machinery products, the production of European harmonised standards for IoT, AI-powered advanced robots and autonomous systems is ongoing... in order to offer a level playing field and a competitive advantage to European manufacturers... under the Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC and the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU[6] — this is where technical influence is actually exercised, not through legislative lobbying.

The Commission's own stakeholder consultation on the Data Act shows industrial data-holders already organised around a clear position worth aligning with: they want a single unified framework rather than sector carve-outs. Companies obliged to adapt their data systems under the Data Act acknowledged compliance costs but saw the requirements as manageable, especially when building on existing data-sharing infrastructure, and rejected calls to replace the Act with sector-specific rules, favouring a unified framework to avoid regulatory fragmentation[7]. That consultation record is a coalition door, not a hypothetical.

**Lobbying focus:** the highest-value venue is the ongoing European Standardisation Organisation work programme on harmonised IoT and machinery standards — contributing technical input here secures presumption-of-conformity benefits directly, at a scale this company can execute without needing to confront any single dominant rival.

**Coalitions:**
- Data Act stakeholder-consultation respondents (data holders/manufacturers) who publicly rejected sector-specific fragmentation — a documented, aligned industry position.
- Standardisation-body technical working groups drafting IoT/machinery harmonised standards, which explicitly aim to give European manufacturers a competitive edge.
- SME/industry associations that rated fragmentation risk 4.38/5 in the Commission's product-security public consultation, signalling broad manufacturer consensus for EU-level harmonisation over national patchwork rules.

**Watchlist:**
- Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 becomes the binding text from 20 January 2027 — the conformity framework changes under this deadline.
- Digital Omnibus proposals (52025PC0836, 52025PC0837) simplifying AI Act sandbox access and Data Act re-use conditions for large enterprises — track for compliance-cost shifts.
- Ongoing ENISA/CSIRT vulnerability-database rollout under CRA Article 12(2) coordination with NIS2 — operational reporting channel to establish now.
- Continued European Standardisation Organisation harmonised-standards drafting for IoT and combined-product safety — direct technical engagement window.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|
| GDPR (32016R0679) | Company handles no personal data. | Processing employee, customer or end-user personal data at scale. |
| AI Act (32024R1689) | Company uses no AI systems. | Adding AI-based analytics or decision features to sensors/controllers. |
| DMA (32022R1925) | Not a designated gatekeeper; no core platform services. | Operating a qualifying core platform service above Art. 3(2) thresholds. |
| DSA (32022R2065) | Not a provider of intermediary/hosting services. | Launching an online marketplace or hosting platform. |
| DORA (32022R2554) | Not a financial entity. | Entering regulated financial services. |
| MiCA (32023R1114) | No crypto-asset activity of any kind. | Issuing or servicing crypto-assets. |
| P2B Regulation (32019R1150) | Not a provider of online intermediation services. | Operating a B2B online marketplace or app store. |
| eIDAS2 (32024R1183) | Not a digital identity wallet or trust service provider. | Becoming a notified Wallet or Qualified Trust Service Provider. |
| EMFA (32024R1083) | Not a media service provider. | Entering media/broadcast device markets. |
| ePrivacy Directive (32002L0058) | B2B industrial sales, no consumer electronic-communications tracking. | Selling consumer-facing connected devices with tracking features. |
| CER Directive (32022L2557) | Not an operator of designated critical infrastructure. | Being designated a critical entity by a Member State. |
| Chips Act (32023R1781) | Not a semiconductor manufacturer. | Entering chip design/fabrication. |
| Data Governance Act (32022R0868) | Not a data intermediary or data-altruism organisation. | Operating a data-sharing intermediary service. |
| Consumer Rights Directive (32011L0083) | Sells exclusively to industrial B2B customers, not consumers. | Launching direct-to-consumer sales channels. |
| Green Claims Directive (32024L0825) | No consumer-facing environmental comparison claims. | Marketing sustainability comparisons to consumers. |
| European Accessibility Act (32019L0882) | Products/services not covered consumer accessibility categories. | Selling in-scope consumer digital products or services. |
| Web Accessibility Directive (32016L2102) | Not a public sector body. | N/A absent a public-sector role. |
| Open Data Directive (32019L1024) | Not a public sector body holding public-sector information. | N/A absent a public-sector role. |
| Package Travel Directive (32015L2302) | Not a travel organiser or retailer. | Entering travel services. |
| EHR Regulation (32025R0327) | No electronic health record systems. | Entering health IT/EHR markets. |

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Panel — Regional Logistics & Warehousing Operator

**A single obligation carries real weight — NIS2 cybersecurity duties as a courier/logistics operator — while the rest of the EU digital-regulation canon (GDPR, AI Act, DSA, DMA, Data Act and the platform-economy files) does not touch this business as described.**

## Bottom line

- NIS2 is In Scope, Prio 2: last-mile delivery places the company in the "postal and courier services" sector, and its medium-enterprise size trips the Directive's size-cap trigger — this is bounded, resourceable compliance work, not an existential risk this year.
- No Prio 1 exposure — nothing here requires immediate action.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) | 2 | **In Scope** | Postal and courier services fall within NIS2's covered sectors, and the Directive applies via a uniform size threshold: a size-cap rule, whereby all entities which qualify as medium-sized enterprises under Article 2 of the Annex to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC, or exceed the ceilings for medium-sized enterprises, and which operate within the sectors and provide the types of service or carry out the activities covered by this Directive fall within its scope[1]. As a medium-sized courier/last-mile operator, this company clears that bar and owes risk-management and incident-reporting obligations. |
| Critical Entities Resilience Directive (32022L2557) | 3 | **Monitor** | CER designation is Member-State-driven per sector list, and postal/courier is not among the CER-listed critical sectors retrieved (energy, transport, banking, financial infrastructure, health, water, hydrogen). Hinges on whether a future national CER designation sweeps in courier/logistics as critical infrastructure — confirm with the German competent authority. |

NIS2 is the file that actually matters here, and its enforcement reality is still forming. Germany has not yet fully transposed the Directive into national law (the NIS2 Cooperation Group process, drawing on structures established by Directive (EU) 2016/1148 of the European Parliament and of the Council ('the Cooperation Group') brings together competent authorities in order to support and facilitate cooperation, in particular by providing strategic guidance for the activities of the Computer Security Incident Response Teams network[2], continues to run under the predecessor NIS regime pending national implementation). This does not make NIS2 optional — the size-cap criterion in the Directive text is self-executing once national law catches up, and courier/logistics operators of this scale should not wait for the German transposition act to start baseline risk-management work (incident-reporting contact points, supply-chain security review, basic cyber hygiene). Treat 2026 as the compliance-build year, not the enforcement year.

## Political landscape & strategic play

NIS2 implementation in Germany runs through the Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI), which is designated to be the national competent authority and single point of contact once the NIS2UmsuCG transposition act is finalised; at EU level, DG CNECT and ENISA jointly steer implementing guidance and the sectoral scoping methodology that will determine exactly how "postal and courier services" gets applied to logistics operators. The Cooperation Group structure that predates NIS2 continues to function as the venue where Member States align on scope questions, and it is the practical channel through which sector associations get clarity on edge cases like regional freight/warehousing operators that also run last-mile delivery.

**Lobbying focus.** The highest-value engagement for a company this size is not Brussels but the German transposition process: submitting scope-clarification input to BSI or the responsible ministry on how "courier services" is defined for medium-sized regional operators, ideally through a national logistics or transport trade association rather than alone. A direct filing or unilateral position paper is disproportionate at this scale; coalition input through an existing trade body is the realistic and executable ask.

**Coalitions.** The retrieved sources do not name a logistics-sector trade association or complainant group organised specifically around NIS2 scope for courier/warehousing operators — this is a gap to fill with client-side research rather than an invented coalition.

**Watchlist.**
- Finalisation of Germany's NIS2 transposition act (NIS2UmsuCG) — sets the concrete national deadline and BSI registration/reporting mechanics that currently remain pending.
- Any ENISA or Cooperation Group sectoral guidance clarifying which logistics/courier activities count as "postal and courier services" under NIS2 Annex II — directly determines in/out-of-scope status.
- Any future amendment to the CER Directive's sectoral annex that could add logistics/transport-adjacent activities to the critical-entities list, which would upgrade the current Monitor verdict.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Early-Stage B2B SaaS Panel

**GDPR is the only live compliance obligation this two-person startup carries today; every other EU digital-acquis instrument retrieved is either inapplicable at this size and activity profile or a pure future-watch item.**

## Bottom line
- ACTION: GDPR is In Scope and Prio 1 — the company processes personal data with no dedicated legal or compliance function, and size gives no exemption beyond a narrow record-keeping derogation.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) | 1 | **In Scope** | The company handles personal data of users/customers. GDPR draws no general size exemption — the Regulation includes a derogation for organisations with fewer than 250 employees only with regard to record-keeping[1], leaving every other controller/processor obligation (lawful basis, security, breach notification, data subject rights) fully applicable regardless of headcount. |
| ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC) | 3 | **Monitor** | Hinges on whether the company deploys cookies or trackers on its marketing site or app — confirm before scoping consent-mechanism obligations. |
| DSA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) | 3 | **Monitor** | Hinges on whether the project-management tool's file/comment storage functions make it a "hosting service" under the DSA's intermediary definitions. Micro/small enterprises are exempted only from the heavier Section 4 online-platform rules — this Section shall not apply to providers of online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders that qualify as micro or small enterprises[2] — but basic hosting due-diligence duties are not size-gated in the retrieved text, so the activity question must be settled first. |

GDPR is the file that actually matters this year, and it is not a soft one. The regime is enforced by a fully operational network of national supervisory authorities coordinated by the European Data Protection Board, and the EU has just moved to make cross-border enforcement faster: a new procedural regulation lets a lead or receiving supervisory authority resolve a cross-border complaint early, before it escalates into a full cooperation procedure, whenever the supervisory authority establishes, based on supporting evidence, that the alleged infringement has been brought to an end[3]. That signals Brussels is tightening the complaint-handling pipeline, not loosening it — a two-person startup with no privacy counsel is exactly the kind of controller that gets caught by a single disgruntled-user complaint rather than a proactive audit. The size-based relief GDPR does offer is narrow and easy to over-rely on: the record-keeping derogation covers documentation obligations only, not the substantive duties around consent, security, or breach notification.

## Political landscape & strategic play

GDPR enforcement runs through the national data protection authority in whichever member state the company establishes itself, with the European Data Protection Board handling consistency across borders. There is no single "rapporteur" to track here — GDPR is settled law, not an active legislative file — but the Commission is actively simplifying adjacent obligations for exactly this size of company. The Digital Omnibus package (proposals 52025PC0836, 52025PC0837, 52025PC0838) is the live vehicle: its impact assessment work drew direct SME input, with SMEs highlighting the challenges faced by smaller players with the AI Act's high-risk rules and calling for more support tools, subsidized conformity assessment, guidance and simplified compliance[4], and separately SMEs and SME associations strongly urging forceful implementation of the Data Act rules[4] while larger incumbents pushed for delay. That divergence tells the company where its natural allies sit in this process.

**Lobbying focus:** the company has no standing yet to engage bilaterally with DG CNECT or DG JUST case teams — it is pre-revenue with no dedicated legal function. The realistic entry point is the Commission's standing SME consultation infrastructure. The precedent channel is the SME Panel run through the European Enterprise Network, which the Commission has used to gather structured feedback on exactly this kind of compliance-burden question — the European Commission deployed a targeted survey to micro, small, and medium enterprises referred to as the "SME Panel Consultation," which was managed by the European Enterprise Network[5]. Feeding a short position statement into the next such consultation, via a national startup or software trade association, is the achievable ask now; direct case-team engagement becomes realistic only once the company crosses into AI Act, Data Act, or NIS2 scope.

**Coalitions:**
- National software/startup trade associations feeding SME Panel-style consultations are the lowest-friction door available at this size.
- Digital Omnibus SME feedback channels already show organized SME-association positions on AI Act and Data Act burden reduction — a natural coalition to join if the company later adopts AI or connects to common data spaces.

**Watchlist:**
- Digital Omnibus proposals (52025PC0836/837/838) — still in negotiation; track for SME/small-mid-cap exemption thresholds that could pre-emptively cover this company if it scales.
- European Business Wallet rollout under the eIDAS2 framework — relevant if the company later needs cross-border digital identity/trust integration for B2B customers.
- Any move by the home-state DPA on breach-notification enforcement against micro-controllers — the concrete trigger event that would elevate GDPR from hygiene to crisis.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|
| AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) | No AI system in use; the Regulation's SME provisions attach to providers or deployers of AI systems[6], a role the company does not hold. | Company builds or deploys any AI feature. |
| DMA (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925) | Not a gatekeeper; designation requires an entrenched, durable core-platform-service position the company does not have. | Commission gatekeeper designation under the Regulation's criteria. |
| DSA — Section 4 platform rules | Micro-enterprise exclusion applies directly per Art. 29. | Loss of micro/small status. |
| Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854) | Targets connected-product/IoT data holders and cloud-switching; a pure project-management SaaS is not a connected product. | Company ships a connected/IoT hardware component. |
| DGA (Regulation (EU) 2022/868) | Not a data intermediation service or data altruism organisation. | Company launches a data-sharing intermediary offering. |
| NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) | Micro enterprises are excluded from the general size-cap rule: a uniform criterion...consist of the application of a size-cap rule, whereby all entities which qualify as medium-sized enterprises...fall within its scope[7]. | Growth past medium-enterprise thresholds or a designated "key role" activity. |
| CRA (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) | Recitals frame obligations around product "manufacturers" placing products with digital elements on the market — facilitate compliance of manufacturers with their obligations[8] — not a pure SaaS delivered as a service. | Company packages downloadable software as a distributed product. |
| DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) | Not a financial entity or critical ICT third-party provider to one. | Company becomes an ICT service provider to regulated financial entities. |
| MiCA (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114) | No crypto-asset activity of any kind. | Company adds crypto-asset issuance or custody features. |
| P2B Regulation (2019/1150) | Customer base is B2B only; the Regulation targets intermediation services connecting business users with consumers. | Company launches a consumer-facing marketplace feature. |
| eIDAS2 (Regulation (EU) 2024/1183) | Not a trust service or wallet provider. | Company becomes a Qualified Trust Service Provider. |
| EMFA (Regulation (EU) 2024/1083) | Not a media service provider. | Company enters media/content-distribution business. |
| ePrivacy Directive — beyond cookie hinge | Only the cookie/tracking question is open; no other ePrivacy obligation applies to a B2B project-management tool. | N/A beyond the noted hinge. |
| Consumer Rights Directive (2011/83/EU) | Customer base is B2B, not consumer-facing. | Company adds a direct-to-consumer product line. |

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Consumer Digital-Health Symptom-Checker Startup

**The AI Act and GDPR are live, binding obligations from day one of market entry — everything else in this profile is a bounded compliance task or a genuine open question, not an existential risk.**

## Bottom line

- AI Act compliance work starts now — as provider of an AI symptom-checker offered to consumers, the company sits inside a regime built around "specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems" and harmonised transparency rules, not a voluntary framework.
- GDPR is a day-one obligation, not a future item — the app processes health data, a special category requiring the highest tier of lawful-basis and security controls under the Regulation.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI Act (32024R1689) | 1 | In Scope | The Regulation lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems in the Union, prohibitions of certain AI practices, specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems, harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems[1]; a consumer-facing AI symptom-checker as a provider falls squarely inside this architecture. |
| GDPR (32016R0679) | 1 | In Scope | The company processes health data, a special category, and the Regulation exists precisely because the scale of the collection and sharing of personal data has increased significantly, and technology allows both private companies and public authorities to make use of personal data on an unprecedented scale[2]. |
| Product Liability Directive (32024L2853) | 2 | In Scope | Software including AI systems is treated as a product for no-fault liability purposes, and a developer or producer of software, including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, should be treated as a manufacturer[3] — direct exposure for an AI symptom-checker. |
| Consumer Rights Directive (32011L0083) | 2 | In Scope | Standard B2C pre-contractual information, withdrawal-right and consumer-protection duties apply to any consumer-facing digital service sold in the EU; the Directive's consumer-protection baseline is reinforced by the ePrivacy Directive's existing rules on unsolicited communications. |
| ePrivacy Directive (32002L0058) | 2 | In Scope | Any consumer app using tracking or communications functionality falls under rules requiring that the protection of the personal data and the privacy of the user of publicly available electronic communications services should be independent of the configuration of the various components necessary to provide the service[4]. |
| Cyber Resilience Act (32024R2847) | 2 | Monitor | Hinges on whether the app qualifies as a "product with digital elements" under CRA rather than a pure SaaS offering — confirm classification before conformity work is scoped. |
| European Health Data Space Reg. (32025R0327) | 2 | Monitor | Hinges on whether the app's outputs constitute an electronic health record subject to EHDS interoperability and access duties, given that Member States should designate relevant digital health authorities for the planning and implementation of standards for access to and transmission of electronic health data[5] — confirm classification with the French digital health authority. |
| Geo-blocking Regulation (32018R0302) | 3 | In Scope | The Regulation applies equally to all traders operating within the Union, since this Regulation should apply equally to all traders, including online marketplaces, operating within the Union[6] — a light-touch non-discrimination duty for EU/FR sales. |

The AI Act is the file that decides everything else. Its purpose is stated as improving the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights[1] — health-adjacent AI is exactly the use case the Regulation was built to catch. The Commission itself frames the enforcement posture as active and evolving: it will work closely with Member States to ensure the consistent implementation and enforcement of the Artificial Intelligence Act and the relevant consumer protection and product safety laws, and the list of prohibited AI practices under the Artificial Intelligence Act will be reviewed annually and updated if new problems are identified[7]. That annual-review mechanism means the compliance target is not static — a symptom-checker judged borderline today can be reclassified without a new legislative act.

## Political landscape & strategic play

The AI Office is consolidating its supervisory reach over AI systems built on general-purpose models, and the Commission has proposed clarifying that Article 75(1) Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 should be modified to bring all AI systems based on general-purpose AI models developed by the same provider within the scope of the AI Office's supervision[8], while sectoral authorities keep responsibility for AI embedded in products already covered by Union harmonisation legislation (such as medical devices). For a symptom-checker, this dual-track split — AI Office versus sectoral medical-device authority — is the single most consequential classification question the company faces, and it is being actively re-drawn at working level inside the AI Office right now.

Separately, the Commission has tabled a package of proposals (52025PC0837, 52025PC0836, 52026PC0502) that touch AI Act implementation, GDPR's legitimate-interest basis for AI training data, and AI Office governance — signalling an active simplification agenda around AI Act/GDPR interaction that a micro provider should track for compliance-cost relief, not just burden.

**Lobbying focus:** the highest-value venue is the AI Office's ongoing guidance process on high-risk classification boundaries for health-adjacent AI, where a documented use case from a genuine micro-provider carries more weight than trade-association noise. The realistic ask is a submission to any open AI Office consultation or SME-support channel, not direct engagement with enforcement staff.

**Coalitions:** the retrieved sources name no health-tech trade association or complainant group organized specifically around this company's issue set — worth building one, but nothing exists yet to join.

**Watchlist:**
- AI Office guidance clarifying the Annex I "sectoral authority" carve-out for medical-device-adjacent AI systems — directly determines which regulator supervises this company.
- Digital Omnibus proposals (52025PC0837, 52026PC0502) moving through co-legislators — could ease AI Act/GDPR compliance costs for micro providers.
- French digital health authority guidance on EHDS classification of consumer health apps — resolves the EHDS Monitor hinge.
- Annual review of the AI Act's prohibited-practices list — could reclassify symptom-checker functionality.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|
| DSA (32022R2065) | Not an intermediary service provider; no third-party content hosting | Adding user-to-user content or messaging features |
| DMA (32022R1925) | Nowhere near gatekeeper thresholds | N/A at micro scale |
| Data Act (32023R2854) | No connected physical product generating device data | Launching a connected wearable or hardware component |
| DGA (32022R0868) | Not a data intermediation service or altruism organisation | Becoming a data-sharing intermediary |
| NIS2 (32022L2555) | Micro enterprise, not an essential/important entity | Growth past micro thresholds or critical-sector designation |
| DORA (32022R2554) | Not a financial entity or ICT third-party provider to one | Selling directly into regulated financial-sector clients |
| MiCA (32023R1114) | No crypto-asset activity of any kind | N/A |
| eIDAS2 (32024R1183) | Not a wallet or trust-service provider | Issuing or relying on EU Digital Identity Wallets |
| EMFA (32024R1083) | Not a media service provider | N/A |
| P2B Regulation (32019R1150) | Protections apply to the company as a business user of app stores, not obligations on it | N/A |
| Cybersecurity Act (32019R0881) | Certification schemes are voluntary, not mandated for this profile | National law mandating a certification scheme |
| Machinery Regulation (32023R1230) | No machinery product | N/A |
| Package Travel Directive (32015L2302) | Not a travel organiser or retailer | N/A |
| EAA (32019L0882) | App is not within enumerated service categories (e-commerce, banking, transport) | Adding e-commerce/payment functionality in scope of the Directive |
| CSRD-linked Directive (32026L0470) | Micro company, below sustainability reporting thresholds | Crossing size thresholds for mandatory reporting |
| GPSR (32023R0988) | Software service, not a physical product | Selling a connected physical device alongside the app |

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Panel (AI SaaS Platform)

**Panel's document-analysis AI system puts it squarely inside the EU AI Act as a provider, with baseline GDPR and product-liability obligations layered on top — no gatekeeper, platform, or sector-specific regime (DMA, DSA, NIS2, CRA, DORA, MiCA) currently reaches a B2B enterprise API of this kind.**

## Bottom line
- AI Act is Prio 1: Panel is a confirmed AI system provider under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and the specific conformity-assessment burden hinges on whether its document-analysis outputs feed Annex III high-risk use cases (e.g., employment or credit decisions) — this determination is unresolved and drives the compliance roadmap.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI Act (Reg. 2024/1689) | 1 | **In Scope** | Panel's stated role is AI system provider; the Regulation governs "the development, placement on the market and use of products and services embedding AI technology" to establish harmonised rules on the development, placement on the market and use of products and services embedding AI technology or stand-alone AI applications in the Union[1]. If Panel's document-analysis engine incorporates a third-party foundation model, value-chain cooperation duties on model suppliers and integrators also attach. |
| GDPR (Reg. 2016/679) | 2 | **In Scope** | Panel processes personal data within customer documents as a B2B processor/controller; standard accountability, DPIA, and cross-border enforcement cooperation rules apply as routine hygiene, not an existential risk. |
| Product Liability Directive (Dir. 2024/2853) | 2 | **In Scope** | The Directive treats software providers as manufacturers for no-fault liability purposes: A developer or producer of software, including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council, should be treated as a manufacturer.[2] Panel's AI system is squarely captured. |

The AI Act is the one file that determines Panel's actual compliance workload for the next two years. The Regulation created an AI Office to police the highest-risk tier of obligations, and a pending Commission proposal would widen that office's reach: sectoral authorities continue to remain responsible for the supervision of AI systems related to products covered by that Union harmonisation legislation, Article 75(1) Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 should be modified to bring all AI systems based on general-purpose AI models developed by the same provider within the scope of the AI Office's supervision.[3] That signals tightening, not loosening, enforcement architecture even as simplification debates continue elsewhere. Separately, if Panel's document-analysis pipeline incorporates externally sourced models or components, the value-chain provisions matter directly: all relevant third parties, in particular those that are involved in the development, sale and the commercial supply of software tools, components, pre-trained models or data incorporated into the AI system, or providers of network services, should… make available the required information, training or expertise and cooperate, as appropriate, with providers to enable their control over all compliance relevant aspects of the AI system that falls under this Regulation.[4] Confirming Annex III exposure and mapping every upstream model supplier's disclosure obligations are the two concrete workstreams that resolve the Monitor-adjacent uncertainty into a fixed compliance plan.

## Political landscape & strategic play

The AI Office, housed within the Commission's DG CNECT, is the working-level body that will decide how document-analysis use cases are classified and how GPAI-based systems are supervised; the pending amendment proposal explicitly recasts its mandate to cover the role of the AI Office in monitoring and supervising compliance of such AI systems with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, while excluding AI systems related to products covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I to that Regulation[3]. On the data-protection side, national DPAs (in Germany, the federal and state authorities) enforce GDPR under EDPB coordination, which issues guidance to keep supervisory practice consistent across cross-border processing cases.

**Lobbying focus:** the highest-value venue is the AI Office's ongoing guidance and Code-of-Practice process for GPAI-based systems and Annex III classification criteria. A medium-sized B2B provider's realistic ask is participation in the Commission's stakeholder consultation rounds on high-risk classification guidance for enterprise document-processing use cases, not a formal complaint — Panel has no standing to escalate against a named incumbent, since none is identified in its profile.

**Coalitions:** the retrieved sources name no trade association, complainant group, or peer company already organized around Panel's specific AI Act or product-liability exposure, and Panel's own profile names no competitor — this is a genuine gap to fill through direct engagement rather than joining an existing bloc.

**Watchlist:**
- AI Office supervisory-scope amendment (proposal 2025/0500 family, doc 52025PC0836) — determines whether GPAI-based systems Panel deploys fall under central AI Office oversight rather than national market surveillance.
- National transposition of the Product Liability Directive (2024/2853) into German civil law — confirm implementing-statute status and effective date.
- AI value-chain disclosure practice under Article-level cooperation duties (doc 52023AP0236) — confirm which upstream model suppliers Panel relies on and their disclosure posture.
- Continued AI Office guidance on Annex III high-risk classification — the single fact that reclassifies Panel's entire AI Act workload if document-analysis outputs feed employment, credit, or similarly listed decisions.

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Industrial IoT Manufacturer (Connected Sensors & Controllers)

**The Cyber Resilience Act is now the company's binding compliance centre of gravity as a manufacturer of products with digital elements, with the Machinery Directive, NIS2 and the Data Act layered on top as bounded but real obligations — no AI Act, GDPR, DMA or DSA exposure exists given the no-AI, no-personal-data, B2B profile.**

## Bottom line

- CRA compliance (vulnerability handling, conformity assessment, technical documentation) is Prio 1 because connected sensors and controllers are squarely "products with digital elements" under a regime already in force with active ENISA/CSIRT enforcement infrastructure — this is not a future file, it is live obligation-building work now.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cyber Resilience Act (32024R2847) | 1 | **In Scope** | Connected sensors/controllers are products with digital elements; the Regulation requires manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and work with CSIRTs designated as coordinators, which provide helpdesk support in relation to the reporting obligations to manufacturers[1], alongside conformity documentation and, where used, authorised-representative mandates. |
| Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC (33006L0042) | 2 | **In Scope** | The Directive's definition of "manufacturer" means any natural or legal person who designs and/or manufactures machinery or partly completed machinery covered by this Directive and is responsible for the conformity of the machinery or the partly completed machinery"[2] covers controllers and safety-relevant components for factory automation; the Directive remains the binding text now. Its successor, the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, applies only from 20 January 2027 — plan the transition, do not treat it as current law yet. |
| NIS2 Directive (32022L2555) | 2 | **In Scope** | The Directive's sector annex names manufacture of computer, electronic and optical products, manufacture of electrical equipment, and manufacture of machinery and equipment n.e.c.[3] as covered activities, and the company's large size places it above the important-entity threshold. |
| Data Act (32023R2854) | 2 | **In Scope** | As a large manufacturer of connected products, none of the Data Act's microenterprise/small-enterprise design-obligation carve-outs apply — those exemptions and the one-year transitional period are reserved for enterprises that qualify as micro, small, or newly-medium given the current state of technology, it would be overly burdensome on microenterprises and small enterprises to impose further design obligations... A transitional period should apply to an enterprise that has qualified as a medium-sized enterprise for less than one year[4] — full data-access and sharing obligations apply from day one. |
| Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU | 2 | **Monitor** | Hinges on whether the connected sensors/controllers incorporate radio transmission (vs. wired fieldbus only) — confirm product-line radio functionality before scoping conformity assessment. |
| EU Cybersecurity Act (32019R0881) | 3 | **Monitor** | Certification is currently voluntary, but connected and automated cars, electronic medical devices, industrial automation control systems and smart grids are only some examples of sectors in which certification is already widely used or is likely to be used in the near future[5], and Member States retain power to make schemes mandatory nationally. |

The Cyber Resilience Act deserves the most attention because it is a fully binding Regulation with an operating enforcement chain, not a proposal. ENISA maintains the coordinated vulnerability database and works directly with manufacturers on disclosure, while national CSIRTs are tasked with helpdesk support specifically aimed at smaller suppliers, signalling the Commission expects broad manufacturer coverage rather than a narrow niche regime. The obligations attach to the product category — connected devices with digital elements — not to company size beyond the microenterprise carve-outs the Act does not extend to a large manufacturer. Treat this as the anchor compliance file for 2025-2026 procurement, engineering and legal workstreams alike.

## Political landscape & strategic play

Cybersecurity and product-safety rulemaking for connected industrial equipment sits across two Commission services: DG CNECT drives CRA implementation and delegated acts, while DG GROW owns the Machinery Regulation transition and Radio Equipment Directive enforcement. National market surveillance authorities and CSIRTs designated as coordinators under the CRA are the operational contact points a manufacturer will actually deal with on vulnerability reporting, not Brussels-level political actors. On standardisation, the European Standardisation Organisations are actively drafting the harmonised standards that will carry presumption of conformity for IoT and machinery products, the production of European harmonised standards for IoT, AI-powered advanced robots and autonomous systems is ongoing... in order to offer a level playing field and a competitive advantage to European manufacturers... under the Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC and the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU[6] — this is where technical influence is actually exercised, not through legislative lobbying.

The Commission's own stakeholder consultation on the Data Act shows industrial data-holders already organised around a clear position worth aligning with: they want a single unified framework rather than sector carve-outs. Companies obliged to adapt their data systems under the Data Act acknowledged compliance costs but saw the requirements as manageable, especially when building on existing data-sharing infrastructure, and rejected calls to replace the Act with sector-specific rules, favouring a unified framework to avoid regulatory fragmentation[7]. That consultation record is a coalition door, not a hypothetical.

**Lobbying focus:** the highest-value venue is the ongoing European Standardisation Organisation work programme on harmonised IoT and machinery standards — contributing technical input here secures presumption-of-conformity benefits directly, at a scale this company can execute without needing to confront any single dominant rival.

**Coalitions:**
- Data Act stakeholder-consultation respondents (data holders/manufacturers) who publicly rejected sector-specific fragmentation — a documented, aligned industry position.
- Standardisation-body technical working groups drafting IoT/machinery harmonised standards, which explicitly aim to give European manufacturers a competitive edge.
- SME/industry associations that rated fragmentation risk 4.38/5 in the Commission's product-security public consultation, signalling broad manufacturer consensus for EU-level harmonisation over national patchwork rules.

**Watchlist:**
- Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 becomes the binding text from 20 January 2027 — the conformity framework changes under this deadline.
- Digital Omnibus proposals (52025PC0836, 52025PC0837) simplifying AI Act sandbox access and Data Act re-use conditions for large enterprises — track for compliance-cost shifts.
- Ongoing ENISA/CSIRT vulnerability-database rollout under CRA Article 12(2) coordination with NIS2 — operational reporting channel to establish now.
- Continued European Standardisation Organisation harmonised-standards drafting for IoT and combined-product safety — direct technical engagement window.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|
| GDPR (32016R0679) | Company handles no personal data. | Processing employee, customer or end-user personal data at scale. |
| AI Act (32024R1689) | Company uses no AI systems. | Adding AI-based analytics or decision features to sensors/controllers. |
| DMA (32022R1925) | Not a designated gatekeeper; no core platform services. | Operating a qualifying core platform service above Art. 3(2) thresholds. |
| DSA (32022R2065) | Not a provider of intermediary/hosting services. | Launching an online marketplace or hosting platform. |
| DORA (32022R2554) | Not a financial entity. | Entering regulated financial services. |
| MiCA (32023R1114) | No crypto-asset activity of any kind. | Issuing or servicing crypto-assets. |
| P2B Regulation (32019R1150) | Not a provider of online intermediation services. | Operating a B2B online marketplace or app store. |
| eIDAS2 (32024R1183) | Not a digital identity wallet or trust service provider. | Becoming a notified Wallet or Qualified Trust Service Provider. |
| EMFA (32024R1083) | Not a media service provider. | Entering media/broadcast device markets. |
| ePrivacy Directive (32002L0058) | B2B industrial sales, no consumer electronic-communications tracking. | Selling consumer-facing connected devices with tracking features. |
| CER Directive (32022L2557) | Not an operator of designated critical infrastructure. | Being designated a critical entity by a Member State. |
| Chips Act (32023R1781) | Not a semiconductor manufacturer. | Entering chip design/fabrication. |
| Data Governance Act (32022R0868) | Not a data intermediary or data-altruism organisation. | Operating a data-sharing intermediary service. |
| Consumer Rights Directive (32011L0083) | Sells exclusively to industrial B2B customers, not consumers. | Launching direct-to-consumer sales channels. |
| Green Claims Directive (32024L0825) | No consumer-facing environmental comparison claims. | Marketing sustainability comparisons to consumers. |
| European Accessibility Act (32019L0882) | Products/services not covered consumer accessibility categories. | Selling in-scope consumer digital products or services. |
| Web Accessibility Directive (32016L2102) | Not a public sector body. | N/A absent a public-sector role. |
| Open Data Directive (32019L1024) | Not a public sector body holding public-sector information. | N/A absent a public-sector role. |
| Package Travel Directive (32015L2302) | Not a travel organiser or retailer. | Entering travel services. |
| EHR Regulation (32025R0327) | No electronic health record systems. | Entering health IT/EHR markets. |

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Panel — Regional Logistics & Warehousing Operator

**A single obligation carries real weight — NIS2 cybersecurity duties as a courier/logistics operator — while the rest of the EU digital-regulation canon (GDPR, AI Act, DSA, DMA, Data Act and the platform-economy files) does not touch this business as described.**

## Bottom line

- NIS2 is In Scope, Prio 2: last-mile delivery places the company in the "postal and courier services" sector, and its medium-enterprise size trips the Directive's size-cap trigger — this is bounded, resourceable compliance work, not an existential risk this year.
- No Prio 1 exposure — nothing here requires immediate action.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) | 2 | **In Scope** | Postal and courier services fall within NIS2's covered sectors, and the Directive applies via a uniform size threshold: a size-cap rule, whereby all entities which qualify as medium-sized enterprises under Article 2 of the Annex to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC, or exceed the ceilings for medium-sized enterprises, and which operate within the sectors and provide the types of service or carry out the activities covered by this Directive fall within its scope[1]. As a medium-sized courier/last-mile operator, this company clears that bar and owes risk-management and incident-reporting obligations. |
| Critical Entities Resilience Directive (32022L2557) | 3 | **Monitor** | CER designation is Member-State-driven per sector list, and postal/courier is not among the CER-listed critical sectors retrieved (energy, transport, banking, financial infrastructure, health, water, hydrogen). Hinges on whether a future national CER designation sweeps in courier/logistics as critical infrastructure — confirm with the German competent authority. |

NIS2 is the file that actually matters here, and its enforcement reality is still forming. Germany has not yet fully transposed the Directive into national law (the NIS2 Cooperation Group process, drawing on structures established by Directive (EU) 2016/1148 of the European Parliament and of the Council ('the Cooperation Group') brings together competent authorities in order to support and facilitate cooperation, in particular by providing strategic guidance for the activities of the Computer Security Incident Response Teams network[2], continues to run under the predecessor NIS regime pending national implementation). This does not make NIS2 optional — the size-cap criterion in the Directive text is self-executing once national law catches up, and courier/logistics operators of this scale should not wait for the German transposition act to start baseline risk-management work (incident-reporting contact points, supply-chain security review, basic cyber hygiene). Treat 2026 as the compliance-build year, not the enforcement year.

## Political landscape & strategic play

NIS2 implementation in Germany runs through the Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI), which is designated to be the national competent authority and single point of contact once the NIS2UmsuCG transposition act is finalised; at EU level, DG CNECT and ENISA jointly steer implementing guidance and the sectoral scoping methodology that will determine exactly how "postal and courier services" gets applied to logistics operators. The Cooperation Group structure that predates NIS2 continues to function as the venue where Member States align on scope questions, and it is the practical channel through which sector associations get clarity on edge cases like regional freight/warehousing operators that also run last-mile delivery.

**Lobbying focus.** The highest-value engagement for a company this size is not Brussels but the German transposition process: submitting scope-clarification input to BSI or the responsible ministry on how "courier services" is defined for medium-sized regional operators, ideally through a national logistics or transport trade association rather than alone. A direct filing or unilateral position paper is disproportionate at this scale; coalition input through an existing trade body is the realistic and executable ask.

**Coalitions.** The retrieved sources do not name a logistics-sector trade association or complainant group organised specifically around NIS2 scope for courier/warehousing operators — this is a gap to fill with client-side research rather than an invented coalition.

**Watchlist.**
- Finalisation of Germany's NIS2 transposition act (NIS2UmsuCG) — sets the concrete national deadline and BSI registration/reporting mechanics that currently remain pending.
- Any ENISA or Cooperation Group sectoral guidance clarifying which logistics/courier activities count as "postal and courier services" under NIS2 Annex II — directly determines in/out-of-scope status.
- Any future amendment to the CER Directive's sectoral annex that could add logistics/transport-adjacent activities to the critical-entities list, which would upgrade the current Monitor verdict.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|
| GDPR (32016R0679) | Company profile states no personal data handling. | Starts processing customer, employee or driver personal data at scale. |
| ePrivacy Directive (32002L0058) | No electronic communications service offered to the public; no personal data processing claimed. | Launches a public electronic communications or direct-marketing service. |
| AI Act (32024R1689) | Company profile states no AI use. | Deploys an AI system, including for route optimisation or automated decision-making on workers. |
| DMA (32022R1925) | Not a core platform service provider; no gatekeeper designation possible at this scale. | Becomes a designated gatekeeper under Art. 3(2) thresholds. |
| DSA (32022R2065) | No online platform, marketplace or hosting service operated. | Launches a consumer-facing digital marketplace or platform. |
| Data Act (32023R2854) | No connected products manufactured; internal ops software only, no third-party data-sharing obligations triggered. | Deploys connected/IoT hardware in warehousing operations. |
| Data Governance Act (32022R0868) | No data intermediation or altruism service provided. | Begins operating a data-sharing intermediary service. |
| CRA (32024R2847) | Not a manufacturer of products with digital elements. | Starts distributing connected hardware under its own brand. |

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Early-Stage B2B SaaS Panel

**GDPR is the only live compliance obligation this two-person startup carries today; every other EU digital-acquis instrument retrieved is either inapplicable at this size and activity profile or a pure future-watch item.**

## Bottom line
- ACTION: GDPR is In Scope and Prio 1 — the company processes personal data with no dedicated legal or compliance function, and size gives no exemption beyond a narrow record-keeping derogation.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) | 1 | **In Scope** | The company handles personal data of users/customers. GDPR draws no general size exemption — the Regulation includes a derogation for organisations with fewer than 250 employees only with regard to record-keeping[1], leaving every other controller/processor obligation (lawful basis, security, breach notification, data subject rights) fully applicable regardless of headcount. |
| ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC) | 3 | **Monitor** | Hinges on whether the company deploys cookies or trackers on its marketing site or app — confirm before scoping consent-mechanism obligations. |
| DSA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) | 3 | **Monitor** | Hinges on whether the project-management tool's file/comment storage functions make it a "hosting service" under the DSA's intermediary definitions. Micro/small enterprises are exempted only from the heavier Section 4 online-platform rules — this Section shall not apply to providers of online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders that qualify as micro or small enterprises[2] — but basic hosting due-diligence duties are not size-gated in the retrieved text, so the activity question must be settled first. |

GDPR is the file that actually matters this year, and it is not a soft one. The regime is enforced by a fully operational network of national supervisory authorities coordinated by the European Data Protection Board, and the EU has just moved to make cross-border enforcement faster: a new procedural regulation lets a lead or receiving supervisory authority resolve a cross-border complaint early, before it escalates into a full cooperation procedure, whenever the supervisory authority establishes, based on supporting evidence, that the alleged infringement has been brought to an end[3]. That signals Brussels is tightening the complaint-handling pipeline, not loosening it — a two-person startup with no privacy counsel is exactly the kind of controller that gets caught by a single disgruntled-user complaint rather than a proactive audit. The size-based relief GDPR does offer is narrow and easy to over-rely on: the record-keeping derogation covers documentation obligations only, not the substantive duties around consent, security, or breach notification.

## Political landscape & strategic play

GDPR enforcement runs through the national data protection authority in whichever member state the company establishes itself, with the European Data Protection Board handling consistency across borders. There is no single "rapporteur" to track here — GDPR is settled law, not an active legislative file — but the Commission is actively simplifying adjacent obligations for exactly this size of company. The Digital Omnibus package (proposals 52025PC0836, 52025PC0837, 52025PC0838) is the live vehicle: its impact assessment work drew direct SME input, with SMEs highlighting the challenges faced by smaller players with the AI Act's high-risk rules and calling for more support tools, subsidized conformity assessment, guidance and simplified compliance[4], and separately SMEs and SME associations strongly urging forceful implementation of the Data Act rules[4] while larger incumbents pushed for delay. That divergence tells the company where its natural allies sit in this process.

**Lobbying focus:** the company has no standing yet to engage bilaterally with DG CNECT or DG JUST case teams — it is pre-revenue with no dedicated legal function. The realistic entry point is the Commission's standing SME consultation infrastructure. The precedent channel is the SME Panel run through the European Enterprise Network, which the Commission has used to gather structured feedback on exactly this kind of compliance-burden question — the European Commission deployed a targeted survey to micro, small, and medium enterprises referred to as the "SME Panel Consultation," which was managed by the European Enterprise Network[5]. Feeding a short position statement into the next such consultation, via a national startup or software trade association, is the achievable ask now; direct case-team engagement becomes realistic only once the company crosses into AI Act, Data Act, or NIS2 scope.

**Coalitions:**
- National software/startup trade associations feeding SME Panel-style consultations are the lowest-friction door available at this size.
- Digital Omnibus SME feedback channels already show organized SME-association positions on AI Act and Data Act burden reduction — a natural coalition to join if the company later adopts AI or connects to common data spaces.

**Watchlist:**
- Digital Omnibus proposals (52025PC0836/837/838) — still in negotiation; track for SME/small-mid-cap exemption thresholds that could pre-emptively cover this company if it scales.
- European Business Wallet rollout under the eIDAS2 framework — relevant if the company later needs cross-border digital identity/trust integration for B2B customers.
- Any move by the home-state DPA on breach-notification enforcement against micro-controllers — the concrete trigger event that would elevate GDPR from hygiene to crisis.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|
| AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) | No AI system in use; the Regulation's SME provisions attach to providers or deployers of AI systems[6], a role the company does not hold. | Company builds or deploys any AI feature. |
| DMA (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925) | Not a gatekeeper; designation requires an entrenched, durable core-platform-service position the company does not have. | Commission gatekeeper designation under the Regulation's criteria. |
| DSA — Section 4 platform rules | Micro-enterprise exclusion applies directly per Art. 29. | Loss of micro/small status. |
| Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854) | Targets connected-product/IoT data holders and cloud-switching; a pure project-management SaaS is not a connected product. | Company ships a connected/IoT hardware component. |
| DGA (Regulation (EU) 2022/868) | Not a data intermediation service or data altruism organisation. | Company launches a data-sharing intermediary offering. |
| NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) | Micro enterprises are excluded from the general size-cap rule: a uniform criterion...consist of the application of a size-cap rule, whereby all entities which qualify as medium-sized enterprises...fall within its scope[7]. | Growth past medium-enterprise thresholds or a designated "key role" activity. |
| CRA (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) | Recitals frame obligations around product "manufacturers" placing products with digital elements on the market — facilitate compliance of manufacturers with their obligations[8] — not a pure SaaS delivered as a service. | Company packages downloadable software as a distributed product. |
| DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) | Not a financial entity or critical ICT third-party provider to one. | Company becomes an ICT service provider to regulated financial entities. |
| MiCA (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114) | No crypto-asset activity of any kind. | Company adds crypto-asset issuance or custody features. |
| P2B Regulation (2019/1150) | Customer base is B2B only; the Regulation targets intermediation services connecting business users with consumers. | Company launches a consumer-facing marketplace feature. |
| eIDAS2 (Regulation (EU) 2024/1183) | Not a trust service or wallet provider. | Company becomes a Qualified Trust Service Provider. |
| EMFA (Regulation (EU) 2024/1083) | Not a media service provider. | Company enters media/content-distribution business. |
| ePrivacy Directive — beyond cookie hinge | Only the cookie/tracking question is open; no other ePrivacy obligation applies to a B2B project-management tool. | N/A beyond the noted hinge. |
| Consumer Rights Directive (2011/83/EU) | Customer base is B2B, not consumer-facing. | Company adds a direct-to-consumer product line. |
