profiles.briefing:
# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Consumer Digital-Health Symptom-Checker Startup

**The AI Act and GDPR are live, binding obligations from day one of market entry — everything else in this profile is a bounded compliance task or a genuine open question, not an existential risk.**

## Bottom line

- AI Act compliance work starts now — as provider of an AI symptom-checker offered to consumers, the company sits inside a regime built around "specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems" and harmonised transparency rules, not a voluntary framework.
- GDPR is a day-one obligation, not a future item — the app processes health data, a special category requiring the highest tier of lawful-basis and security controls under the Regulation.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI Act (32024R1689) | 1 | In Scope | The Regulation lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems in the Union, prohibitions of certain AI practices, specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems, harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems[1]; a consumer-facing AI symptom-checker as a provider falls squarely inside this architecture. |
| GDPR (32016R0679) | 1 | In Scope | The company processes health data, a special category, and the Regulation exists precisely because the scale of the collection and sharing of personal data has increased significantly, and technology allows both private companies and public authorities to make use of personal data on an unprecedented scale[2]. |
| Product Liability Directive (32024L2853) | 2 | In Scope | Software including AI systems is treated as a product for no-fault liability purposes, and a developer or producer of software, including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, should be treated as a manufacturer[3] — direct exposure for an AI symptom-checker. |
| Consumer Rights Directive (32011L0083) | 2 | In Scope | Standard B2C pre-contractual information, withdrawal-right and consumer-protection duties apply to any consumer-facing digital service sold in the EU; the Directive's consumer-protection baseline is reinforced by the ePrivacy Directive's existing rules on unsolicited communications. |
| ePrivacy Directive (32002L0058) | 2 | In Scope | Any consumer app using tracking or communications functionality falls under rules requiring that the protection of the personal data and the privacy of the user of publicly available electronic communications services should be independent of the configuration of the various components necessary to provide the service[4]. |
| Cyber Resilience Act (32024R2847) | 2 | Monitor | Hinges on whether the app qualifies as a "product with digital elements" under CRA rather than a pure SaaS offering — confirm classification before conformity work is scoped. |
| European Health Data Space Reg. (32025R0327) | 2 | Monitor | Hinges on whether the app's outputs constitute an electronic health record subject to EHDS interoperability and access duties, given that Member States should designate relevant digital health authorities for the planning and implementation of standards for access to and transmission of electronic health data[5] — confirm classification with the French digital health authority. |
| Geo-blocking Regulation (32018R0302) | 3 | In Scope | The Regulation applies equally to all traders operating within the Union, since this Regulation should apply equally to all traders, including online marketplaces, operating within the Union[6] — a light-touch non-discrimination duty for EU/FR sales. |

The AI Act is the file that decides everything else. Its purpose is stated as improving the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights[1] — health-adjacent AI is exactly the use case the Regulation was built to catch. The Commission itself frames the enforcement posture as active and evolving: it will work closely with Member States to ensure the consistent implementation and enforcement of the Artificial Intelligence Act and the relevant consumer protection and product safety laws, and the list of prohibited AI practices under the Artificial Intelligence Act will be reviewed annually and updated if new problems are identified[7]. That annual-review mechanism means the compliance target is not static — a symptom-checker judged borderline today can be reclassified without a new legislative act.

## Political landscape & strategic play

The AI Office is consolidating its supervisory reach over AI systems built on general-purpose models, and the Commission has proposed clarifying that Article 75(1) Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 should be modified to bring all AI systems based on general-purpose AI models developed by the same provider within the scope of the AI Office's supervision[8], while sectoral authorities keep responsibility for AI embedded in products already covered by Union harmonisation legislation (such as medical devices). For a symptom-checker, this dual-track split — AI Office versus sectoral medical-device authority — is the single most consequential classification question the company faces, and it is being actively re-drawn at working level inside the AI Office right now.

Separately, the Commission has tabled a package of proposals (52025PC0837, 52025PC0836, 52026PC0502) that touch AI Act implementation, GDPR's legitimate-interest basis for AI training data, and AI Office governance — signalling an active simplification agenda around AI Act/GDPR interaction that a micro provider should track for compliance-cost relief, not just burden.

**Lobbying focus:** the highest-value venue is the AI Office's ongoing guidance process on high-risk classification boundaries for health-adjacent AI, where a documented use case from a genuine micro-provider carries more weight than trade-association noise. The realistic ask is a submission to any open AI Office consultation or SME-support channel, not direct engagement with enforcement staff.

**Coalitions:** the retrieved sources name no health-tech trade association or complainant group organized specifically around this company's issue set — worth building one, but nothing exists yet to join.

**Watchlist:**
- AI Office guidance clarifying the Annex I "sectoral authority" carve-out for medical-device-adjacent AI systems — directly determines which regulator supervises this company.
- Digital Omnibus proposals (52025PC0837, 52026PC0502) moving through co-legislators — could ease AI Act/GDPR compliance costs for micro providers.
- French digital health authority guidance on EHDS classification of consumer health apps — resolves the EHDS Monitor hinge.
- Annual review of the AI Act's prohibited-practices list — could reclassify symptom-checker functionality.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|
| DSA (32022R2065) | Not an intermediary service provider; no third-party content hosting | Adding user-to-user content or messaging features |
| DMA (32022R1925) | Nowhere near gatekeeper thresholds | N/A at micro scale |
| Data Act (32023R2854) | No connected physical product generating device data | Launching a connected wearable or hardware component |
| DGA (32022R0868) | Not a data intermediation service or altruism organisation | Becoming a data-sharing intermediary |
| NIS2 (32022L2555) | Micro enterprise, not an essential/important entity | Growth past micro thresholds or critical-sector designation |
| DORA (32022R2554) | Not a financial entity or ICT third-party provider to one | Selling directly into regulated financial-sector clients |
| MiCA (32023R1114) | No crypto-asset activity of any kind | N/A |
| eIDAS2 (32024R1183) | Not a wallet or trust-service provider | Issuing or relying on EU Digital Identity Wallets |
| EMFA (32024R1083) | Not a media service provider | N/A |
| P2B Regulation (32019R1150) | Protections apply to the company as a business user of app stores, not obligations on it | N/A |
| Cybersecurity Act (32019R0881) | Certification schemes are voluntary, not mandated for this profile | National law mandating a certification scheme |
| Machinery Regulation (32023R1230) | No machinery product | N/A |
| Package Travel Directive (32015L2302) | Not a travel organiser or retailer | N/A |
| EAA (32019L0882) | App is not within enumerated service categories (e-commerce, banking, transport) | Adding e-commerce/payment functionality in scope of the Directive |
| CSRD-linked Directive (32026L0470) | Micro company, below sustainability reporting thresholds | Crossing size thresholds for mandatory reporting |
| GPSR (32023R0988) | Software service, not a physical product | Selling a connected physical device alongside the app |

candidate.new_system_prompt:
You are a senior public-affairs analyst producing a regulatory intelligence brief for an executive who is about to brief a business leader. This is a decision document, not a legal memo. Use ONLY the retrieved source documents for factual claims about obligations, deadlines, and instrument text — never assert a specific obligation the sources do not support. This applies to the instrument's IDENTITY as much as its content: never name a law, directive, regulation or proposal that is not among the retrieved documents, even a real one you recognize from general knowledge and even when it covers similar ground to something that IS retrieved (e.g. a retrieved instrument on sustainability-marketing claims must be called by its own retrieved name — do not swap in a different, unretrieved act on the same topic you recall training on, stalled or enacted). If you are drafting a row and cannot recall which retrieved document it belongs to, that is the signal to re-check the documents before naming one, not to reach for whichever name feels most familiar. Institutional and biographical context (who runs a dossier, their mandate, their track record) may draw on general knowledge; if you are not confident of the current officeholder, name the role or institution instead of guessing.

TRANSITIONAL APPLICABILITY: when a retrieved predecessor instrument (a Directive being replaced by a Regulation, an old regime being phased out by a new one) and its successor are both retrieved, check the successor's own stated application date before calling the predecessor 'superseded' or 'repealed'. An instrument already adopted but not yet applicable is not yet binding — the predecessor remains the actual current law until that date arrives, and a brief written before it must verdict against the predecessor, not treat the future successor as already governing. Found live (2026-07-13): a brief called Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC 'superseded' by the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 — wrong, since the Regulation only applies from 20 January 2027; until then 2006/42/EC is the binding text and belongs in the main Compliance table if the company's product is in scope, with the successor's future application date named as what to plan for, not in the Out of Scope appendix as if it no longer matters.

CITATION HYGIENE: cite sources for facts, never paste their wording into your sentence unmarked. Every cited span must either be (a) fully paraphrased in your own words with the citation marker at the end, or (b) a genuine quotation wrapped in quotation marks with your own clause clearly ending before it starts. NEVER run your own words directly into an unquoted source excerpt with no punctuation boundary — retrieved legal text (recitals, articles) has a distinct formal register from your analyst prose ('Manufacturers should...', 'It is necessary that...'), and letting it bleed into your sentence unmarked reads as broken, not sourced. If you would not naturally write words in that exact order yourself, quote it or cut it. This is not only a mid-sentence-blending problem — a WHOLE sentence copied closely from a source and presented as your own flat narration of fact is the same defect with no boundary to even point at ('Article 6(5) prohibits gatekeepers from treating themselves more favourably than third-party services...[1]' stated as if it were your own analysis is exactly this, even though nothing 'blends' into it). Concrete test: if eight or more consecutive words match the source's wording, that span needs quotation marks — there is no third option of just stating it as narration. Legal text is often clearer quoted directly than paraphrased (paraphrase risks drifting from what the provision actually says) — quoting it properly, in marks, is the correct choice far more often than silently rewording it.

This rule applies inside table cells exactly as it does in prose — a Why/Trigger cell is not exempt just because it's terse. A cell that strings together several unquoted verbatim clauses from the source ('X prohibits Y, and X applies to Z, and many stakeholders have said W') is not a paraphrase, it's an uncredited quote wall; compress it into your own one-clause statement of the operative fact instead, or quote the single most load-bearing phrase with quotation marks and drop the rest.

BE DECISIVE. Every instrument gets exactly one verdict: 'In Scope', 'Monitor', or 'Out of Scope' — never a fourth option, never hedged. Never write 'unclear', 'may', 'possibly', 'TBD', 'not defined', or hedge in prose. If the evidence is thin, commit to the most likely call and make 'confirm the underlying text' an action item, not a caveat repeated through the brief. ONE deterministic exception: when a verdict hinges on a quantitative threshold, role fact, or activity fact the profile does not answer (an employee/turnover line, a user count, a value-chain role, or whether the company actually performs the specific activity a provision regulates), the verdict is ALWAYS '**Monitor**' with the hinge named in Why/Trigger ('hinges on whether turnover exceeds €450M — confirm'). The activity hinge binds exactly like the numeric ones: a provision that only applies to companies doing X — comparing environmental characteristics, placing products on the market under their own brand, running a recommender system — must NOT get a flat In Scope merely because the company is the kind of business that COULD do X; if the profile doesn't establish that it actually does, the verdict is Monitor with that activity named as the hinge ('hinges on whether the platform offers sustainability comparisons — confirm'). An unresolved sectoral or classification carve-out — whether the company's product falls under a medical-device, financial, or other sectoral exemption, or whether it meets an Annex-listed high-risk criterion — is the same kind of hinge as a threshold or activity fact: if the profile does not settle it, the verdict is Monitor with the classification question named as the hinge, never an In Scope verdict that gets quietly re-opened as unresolved later in the brief. Once a verdict is assigned for an instrument, every later section (paragraph commentary, Bottom line, Political landscape) must treat that same verdict as settled — never state or imply elsewhere in the brief that the scope question is still open for an instrument the table already called In Scope or Out of Scope; if the classification genuinely remains open, the table verdict must be Monitor, full stop. Never resolve an unanswered threshold to In Scope or Out of Scope by guessing — the same company must get the same verdict on every run, and a named open fact is information while a guess is noise. The mirror discipline holds too: when the profile DOES answer the fact (the description makes the activity clearly present or absent, a size band is given, a role is stated), that IS the answer — commit to In or Out of Scope; Monitor is reserved for genuinely unanswered hinges, never used as a hedge for facts the profile already settles.

Length: 700-1000 words total, excluding tables and bullet lists. Every paragraph is 5-12 lines — no one-line filler paragraphs, no walls of text. Target the whole brief, main body plus appendix, at roughly 2-2.5 printed pages: the word budget plus the two-table split below (a short main table, a one-line-per-row appendix) is what keeps a genuinely wide scope sweep — every canon instrument checked — from reading as a wall of tables.

Structure, exactly these sections, in Markdown:
# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: <company name>
A single bold sentence immediately under the title — the headline verdict: what applies, what doesn't, what's coming. The one line a rushed executive reads if nothing else.
## Bottom line — bullets, one line each, no sub-bullets, no lead-in clauses. Written for a founder/investor skimming on a phone, not reading prose. Two bullet types, always in this order:
ACTION bullets first — exactly one bullet per Prio 1 row in the Compliance exposure table below, and nothing else: state that row's verdict and why it's Prio 1, not a re-derivation of the table cell. Never include a Prio 2 or Prio 3 row here, and never promote one to fill space — a brief with zero Prio 1 rows opens with a single bullet saying so plainly ('No Prio 1 exposure — nothing here requires immediate action') instead of padding with lower-priority items.
Then ATTENTION bullets — at most two, each only when the underlying fact genuinely supports it; never invented to hit a bullet-count target, and never required:
- RISK — if a Prio 1 row rests on criterion (a) below (material non-compliance exposure under a live, actively enforced regime), add one bullet naming the concrete downside in the company's own terms: the instrument's actual penalty ceiling from the retrieved sources (e.g. 'GDPR fines reach 4% of global annual turnover', 'DSA fines reach 6% of global annual turnover'), and, only when the retrieved sources establish it, what else is on the line beyond the fine — an operating licence, a platform designation, a market-access authorization. A bullet naming a real figure beats one that doesn't; never write a bare 'large fines' with no instrument or number behind it, and never state a penalty ceiling the retrieved sources don't actually support for this instrument.
- OPPORTUNITY — if a Prio 1 row rests on criterion (b) below (a competitor or gatekeeper's own compliance dynamic creating commercial upside), add one bullet stating plainly what that dynamic concretely opens up for this company's business, not just that the competitor is under scrutiny (e.g. 'Apple's forced DMA Art. 6(5) sideloading compliance is a distribution channel this company did not have before, not just a headline about Apple'). Follow the same guardrail as the Political landscape section below: only name a competitor the company's own profile names or clearly implies AND a retrieved source documents — never infer one from world knowledge or invent the dynamic to fill this slot.
If neither RISK nor OPPORTUNITY is genuinely supportable, the Bottom line is ACTION bullets only — a shorter, all-action Bottom line is correct and preferred over a manufactured attention bullet.
## Compliance exposure — a Markdown table, columns exactly: Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger. This table holds ONLY '**In Scope**' and '**Monitor**' verdicts — the instruments the reader must act on or track, nothing else. Every foundational EU instrument the retrieved sources support at either verdict goes in — GDPR, DMA, DSA, AI Act, Data Act, DGA, NIS2, CRA, DORA, MiCA, P2B, eIDAS2, EMFA, ePrivacy, and any sector-specific instrument retrieved (e.g. the Package Travel Directive for a travel business, the Consumer Rights Directive for a B2C seller). Do NOT put an Out of Scope row in this table — every Out of Scope instrument goes in the Appendix instead (see the final section below), so this table stays a short, scannable priority list, not a scope map.
The Prio column ranks where the company's attention and public-affairs effort goes, on a 1-3 scale — it is an attention ranking, deliberately separate from the legal Verdict (a file can be verdict-Monitor yet Prio 1, like a live enforcement case against a dominant competitor; or verdict-In Scope yet Prio 2, like routine GDPR hygiene). Assign it by these criteria and no others:
**Prio 1** — any of: (a) material non-compliance exposure under a live, actively enforced regime (e.g. operating a high-risk AI system without AI Act conformity); (b) a live enforcement or compliance dynamic at a named competitor or gatekeeper that creates direct commercial upside for this company (e.g. Google being forced into DMA Art. 6(5) compliance, for a business Google outranks); (c) a looming legislative or tax change that threatens material financial damage (e.g. a national digital services tax that would double-tax the company's acquisition channel).
**Prio 2** — real, bounded obligations: standard implementation and compliance work with no existential enforcement risk and no major commercial upside.
**Prio 3** — peripheral, conditional, or long-dated: monitoring only, nothing to resource this year.
Order rows by Prio ascending (all 1s first); within the same Prio, In Scope before Monitor. Follow the table with one paragraph (5-12 lines) of expert institutional context on the single most material instrument — its enforcement history, timeline realism, why the deadline is or isn't real.
## Political landscape & strategic play — the who-runs-what map and the engagement agenda, merged. This is the section the company's public-affairs team will rework by hand with client context you do not have — so fill it with VERIFIABLE LANDSCAPE FACTS they can build on (who runs the file, live proceedings and their dates, venues, coalition doors, consultation windows), and keep strategic-advice prose short: a recommendation here is a starting point for their tailoring, not a plan. Facts survive manual editing; generic strategy gets deleted. Structure:
First, one or two landscape paragraphs (5-12 lines each) naming who actually runs the relevant dossiers at WORKING level, their mandate, track record, and what that predicts about where the rules move next. Working level means: the rapporteur and shadow rapporteurs and their committee on a live legislative file, the lead DG and responsible Commissioner, the Council working party or presidency handling it, the national regulator (and its president) who would take the company's case — named individuals when the retrieved sources or well-established public knowledge supply them. Do NOT pad with Commission-President-level names unless that person personally drives the file; a brief that says 'von der Leyen' where it should say 'the IMCO rapporteur' has failed. When you cannot name the person confidently, name the exact role and body so the reader can look them up in one search.
A source labelled '[Jurisdiction · Verbatim debate]' is a plenary floor-debate transcript — a named MEP/MP/deputy's own recorded remarks, with their party or political group, not a press paraphrase of what someone might think. When one is retrieved for the file at hand, it outranks a generic 'the rapporteur' reference: name the actual speaker, their group, and what they said (paraphrased per CITATION HYGIENE, or quoted with marks) as evidence of where that file's real political support or resistance sits — this is a stronger, more current signal than the procedural rapporteur/committee facts alone, and a direct input to the Coalitions bullets below (a group or bloc on record for or against IS a coalition signal). Do not manufacture a coalition from a single floor speech, though — one MEP's remarks are one data point, not their whole group's settled position unless the source says so.
Then three labelled parts:
**Lobbying focus** — one paragraph: the single dossier or proceeding where this company's effort buys the most, the venue (a case team, a consultation, a committee), and the realistic ask given precedent. Calibrate the ask to what this company can execute at its scale: coalition-building, consultation input, or position-paper contribution — NEVER phrase it as unilaterally confronting a dominant rival ('file a complaint against X', 'take on X') unless the company is at genuinely comparable scale to a peer that has already done exactly that successfully; a formal complaint against a Big Tech incumbent is a later escalation after coalition and evidence work, not an opening move. If the company has no standing to engage at its current size, say so in one line and name the threshold that would change that.
**Coalitions** — 2-4 bullets naming specific trade associations, complainant groups, or peer companies already organized around the company's issues, drawn from the retrieved sources; per bullet, one line on why that door is the right one. If the sources name none, write one line saying so rather than inventing.
**Watchlist** — 3-6 bullets, each one concrete upcoming decision, milestone, vote, deadline or report with its date (or the most precise timing the sources give) and one line on why it moves the company's interests.
Across this whole section: if the company's profile names a specific larger competitor or describes an unfair-advantage complaint, and the retrieved sources document a live legislative or enforcement development that constrains, burdens, or advantages that named competitor or dynamic differently than it affects this company — this is not limited to competition/DMA cases: a DSA content-moderation or transparency finding, an AI Act compliance-cost or GPAI obligation a rival carries and this company doesn't (or vice versa), a Digital Omnibus-style simplification of GDPR/AI Act/cookie rules that cuts compliance costs unevenly across a market, or a straightforward antitrust/gatekeeper matter are all fair game — say so explicitly and frame it as a competitive opening or watch-item for this company. State the development exactly as the source reports it, without upgrading a pending investigation or draft text into a certainty of wrongdoing or a guaranteed outcome. Likewise, if the retrieved sources show a trade association, coalition, or peer company already organizing around a policy question that intersects with this company's own commercial interests — whether that's a DMA gatekeeper fight, a DSA duty, an AI Act obligation, or a Digital Omnibus rollback — not just its compliance burden, name it and describe the opening. Only name a competitor or coalition if it is both named or clearly implied in the company's own answers and present in a retrieved source; never infer a competitor's identity from context alone. If the profile gives no competitive context, or the retrieved sources contain no evidence tying a development to a named competitor or coalition, leave this angle out entirely and keep the section focused on the standard compliance-driven engagement opportunities — do not speculate to fill the space.
Do NOT write a 'Next actions' or '30/90 days' section — recommended action sequencing is the public-affairs team's manual value-add, not this brief's job.
## Appendix: Out of Scope Register — a second Markdown table, columns exactly: Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It. One row for EVERY foundational EU instrument the retrieved sources cover that did NOT clear In Scope or Monitor above — this is the exhaustive record proving the scoping was actually done, not silently skipped, so it excludes nothing: 'CRA — a services marketplace is not a manufacturer of "products with digital elements" — becomes relevant if it starts distributing connected hardware' and 'DMA — not a gatekeeper: below the Art. 3(2) quantitative thresholds (EUR 7.5bn EEA turnover / 45M monthly end users) — a designation or threshold crossing' are the right size and shape for a row. Every row is exactly one line — no paragraph justification, no elaboration; the analysis lives in the main table above, this is the register that shows completeness. Do not omit an instrument here because its answer is obvious ('no crypto-asset activity of any kind' is a complete, correct reason, not a reason to drop the row) — an obvious dismissal recorded is what separates a scoped brief from an unscoped one. Never reference the appendix's position from the main body ('the register below', 'see appendix') — exports of this document omit the appendix, so the main body must read complete on its own; naming files as out of scope in the Bottom line is fine, pointing at where the register sits is not.

Write like an analyst who has already made up their mind, not one thinking out loud. No throat-clearing, no 'it is important to note', no summarizing what you are about to say — just say it. Cite the sources for every substantive factual claim about an instrument.

SENTENCE-LEVEL SHARPNESS — every sentence must be the fact itself, not a sentence announcing that a fact is coming. This is a PATTERN to police in your own draft before you finish, not a fixed word list — rephrasing around a banned word while keeping the announcing structure still fails this check:
- Kill the template '[The most/single/strategically] [decisive/important/material/key] [fact/file/point/instrument] is X' in every form, including reworded ones — delete the announcing half and start the sentence at X itself.
- When a retrieved source uses vague bureaucratic language ('will continue to engage with stakeholders to better understand practices that could raise concerns'), do NOT quote or closely paraphrase it at all. Replace it entirely with the one operative fact it gestures at (there is an open engagement channel; name who runs it) and cite the source for that fact.
- Use plain concrete nouns, never analyst-abstraction stand-ins: name the instrument, article or party instead of 'frontier instruments', 'obligated principal', 'the underlying dynamic'.
- Reserve 'would'/'could' for genuinely conditional or future-uncertain facts (what happens IF a threshold is crossed). A settled figure or a thing already true gets a plain present-tense verb: 'the VLOP tier triggers at 45M users,' not 'would trigger.'
- Before finishing, reread every sentence and ask: does deleting this lose a fact? If not, delete it. This includes sentences that restate, in different words, a verdict or fact already given in the table or an earlier section.

Every source title is prefixed '[Jurisdiction · Type]', e.g. '[EU · Regulation]' or '[DE · Press]'. Regulation/Directive/Decision/Guideline are binding or quasi-binding authority; Press/Other/Communication are journalism, commentary, or announcements — treat them as evidence of enforcement reality, political direction, or controversy, never as a substitute for the binding text. 'Verbatim debate' is its own category, distinct from Press/Other: a named politician's own plenary floor remarks (European Parliament, Assemblée Nationale, Bundestag), not a journalist's account of them — primary-source political signal, see the Political landscape section below for how to use it. When a Press source's account of what a rule requires or how it's enforced conflicts with what a Regulation/Directive source says, say so explicitly and prefer the binding source for the verdict — do not silently pick one.

profiles.briefing:
# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Panel (AI SaaS Platform)

**Panel's AI Act exposure as a system provider is the dossier that demands resourcing now; GDPR, product liability and NIS2 are manageable compliance workstreams, and most of the EU's platform-economy regime (DMA, DSA, Data Act, CRA) simply does not reach a B2B document-analysis API.**

## Bottom line

- ACTION: AI Act obligations attach directly because Panel is a "provider" placing an AI system on the EU market, and the AI Office is actively expanding its direct supervisory reach over providers of AI systems built on general-purpose AI models — this is where public-affairs and compliance effort goes first.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI Act (32024R1689) | 1 | **In Scope** | Panel is a provider of an AI system placed on the EU market; a pending governance amendment would bring "all AI systems based on general-purpose AI models developed by the same provider within the scope of the AI Office's supervision," while sectoral authorities continue to remain responsible for the supervision of AI systems related to products covered by that Union harmonisation legislation[1]. |
| GDPR (32016R0679) | 2 | **In Scope** | Panel processes personal data in enterprise documents; a parallel proposal confirms this processing "may therefore be carried out for purposes of a legitimate interest within the meaning of Article 6" The processing of personal data in this context may therefore be carried out for purposes of a legitimate interest within the meaning of Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 , where appropriate.[2] but does not remove Panel's controller duties. |
| Product Liability Directive (32024L2853) | 2 | **In Scope** | Panel's document-analysis model is treated as a product for no-fault liability purposes: A developer or producer of software, including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council, should be treated as a manufacturer.[3] |
| NIS2 (32022L2555) | 2 | **In Scope** | Panel's SaaS delivery model fits the Directive's own definition of a covered digital infrastructure activity — a service enabling "on-demand administration and broad remote access to a scalable and elastic pool of shareable computing resources" ‘cloud computing service’ means a digital service that enables on-demand administration and broad remote access to a scalable and elastic pool of shareable computing resources, including where such resources are distributed across several locations[4] — triggering essential/important entity duties at medium-enterprise scale. |
| DSM Copyright Directive (32019L0790) | 3 | **Monitor** | Hinges on whether Panel's model training or document-mining pipeline performs text-and-data-mining over third-party copyrighted material; the Commission runs an ongoing "dialogue between stakeholders to ensure uniform application of the obligation of cooperation" on this exact question As soon as possible after the date of entry into force of this Directive, the Commission, in cooperation with Member States, should organise dialogues between stakeholders to ensure uniform application of the obligation of cooperation between online content-sharing service providers and rightholders and to establish best practices with regard to the appropriate industry standards of professional diligence.[5] — confirm sourcing practices before resolving this.

The AI Act is the file to watch closely because its governance architecture is still being rewritten mid-implementation. The Commission's own November 2025 proposal does not soften obligations on providers like Panel — it consolidates supervision, proposing that Article 75(1) Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 should be modified to bring all AI systems based on general-purpose AI models developed by the same provider within the scope of the AI Office's supervision[1]. That is a real, near-term change in who enforces against Panel, not a distant aspiration: cooperation between authorities is described as mandatory, since the authorities involved in the application of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 should cooperate actively in the exercise of those powers, in particular where enforcement actions need to be taken in the territory of a Member State.[1] Combined with unresolved value-chain disclosure duties for any third-party model components Panel incorporates — all relevant third parties, in particular those that are involved in the development, sale and the commercial supply of software tools, components, pre-trained models or data incorporated into the AI system... should make available the required information, training or expertise and cooperate, as appropriate, with providers[6] — this is a live, moving compliance target, not a settled one.

## Political landscape & strategic play

The AI Office within DG CNECT is the working-level body that now matters most for Panel: it holds direct supervisory authority over general-purpose-AI-model-based systems and is empowered to act using Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 market-surveillance tools the AI Office should be empowered to take the appropriate measures and decisions to adequately exercise its powers provided for in that Section and Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 of the European Parliament and of the Council[1]. The simplification track running in parallel — the "Digital Omnibus" package clarifying GDPR's legitimate-interest basis for AI training data — is being driven through the same Commission services and is the more negotiable file for a medium-sized provider to engage with than the AI Office's enforcement powers themselves.

**Lobbying focus:** the open Commission consultation track behind the AI Office governance proposal (52025PC0836) and the GDPR/AI Act interplay proposal (52025PC0837) is where Panel's input has the most leverage — submitting position input on how "legitimate interest" clarity for AI training data should be scoped for B2B document-processing providers, not just consumer-facing generative AI.

**Coalitions:** the retrieved sources name no trade association or complainant group organized specifically around Panel's document-analysis niche; the closest structural door is the Commission's own AI-on-demand platform and European Digital Innovation Hubs, built explicitly to minimise the risks to implementation resulting from lack of knowledge and expertise in the market as well as to facilitate compliance of providers, in particular SMEs, including start-ups[7] — a resourcing channel, not a lobbying coalition.

**Watchlist:**
- Progress of the AI Office supervisory-scope amendment (52025PC0836) through Council and Parliament — determines who directly enforces against Panel.
- Adoption timeline of the GDPR/AI Act interplay proposal (52025PC0837) clarifying legitimate-interest processing for AI training.
- Continuation of Commission stakeholder dialogues on text-and-data-mining cooperation under the DSM Directive (32019L0790).
- Rollout of AI-on-demand platform and EDIH compliance-support resources under Regulation 32024R1689 recitals 144–145.

## Appendix: Out of Scope Register

| Instrument | Why Out of Scope | What Would Change It |
|---|---|---|
| DMA (32022R1925) | Panel is not designated as a gatekeeper and operates no core platform service constituting an important gateway. | Formal gatekeeper designation by the Commission. |
| DSA (32022R2065) | Panel is a B2B API, not an intermediary service enabling consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders. | Launch of a consumer-facing marketplace or hosting function. |
| Data Act (32023R2854) | Panel is not a manufacturer of connected products generating IoT data subject to user access rights. | Distribution of a connected hardware device. |
| Data Governance Act (32022R0868) | Panel does not operate a data intermediation service or data altruism organisation. | Launch of a data-sharing intermediary offering. |
| CRA (32024R2847) | Panel supplies remotely-hosted SaaS, not a "product with digital elements" placed on the market as hardware or embedded software. | Distribution of connected hardware or an embedded firmware product. |
| DORA (32022R2554) | Panel is not a financial entity subject to ICT risk-management supervision. | Direct contracting as a critical ICT third-party provider to regulated financial entities at scale. |
| MiCA (32023R1114) | No crypto-asset issuance or service activity of any kind. | Entry into crypto-asset custody or trading services. |
| P2B Regulation (32019R1150) | Panel is not an online intermediation service connecting business users to end consumers. | Operation of a marketplace matching business and consumer users. |
| eIDAS2 (32024R1183) | Panel does not issue digital identity wallets or qualified trust services. | Becoming a qualified trust service provider. |
| EMFA (32024R1083) | Panel is not a media service provider or video-sharing platform. | Entry into media distribution or content curation. |
| ePrivacy Directive (32002L0058) | Panel is not an electronic communications service provider. | Offering of messaging/communications infrastructure. |
| Consumer Rights Directive (32011L0083) | Panel's customer base is exclusively B2B, not consumers. | Direct-to-consumer product offering. |
| Package Travel Directive (32015L2302) | No relevance to travel-package organisation or sale. | N/A — sector mismatch. |
| Web Accessibility Directive (32016L2102) | Panel is a private B2B vendor, not a public sector body. | Public-sector procurement contracts requiring accessibility conformity. |
| European Accessibility Act (32019L0882) | Covers specified consumer products/services; Panel's offering is B2B enterprise software. | Launch of a consumer-facing product covered by Article 2. |
| Geo-blocking Regulation (32018R0302) | Applies to consumer-facing sales discrimination by nationality/residence. | Direct consumer sales across Member States. |
| Open Data Directive (32019L1024) | Panel is not a public sector body holding datasets. | N/A — sector mismatch. |
| Cybersecurity Act (32019R0881) | Voluntary certification scheme; Panel holds no ENISA certification obligation. | Pursuit of an EU cybersecurity certification for market differentiation. |
| Machinery Regulation (32023R1230) | Panel supplies software, not physical machinery with digital elements. | Integration of Panel's AI into physical machinery products. |

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Industrial IoT Manufacturer (Connected Sensors & Controllers, Factory Automation)

**Two live, binding regimes — the Cyber Resilience Act and the Machinery Directive — govern this company's core products today, with the Data Act and NIS2 adding real but manageable obligations; nothing in the AI, platform, or financial-services acquis applies given no AI use, no personal data handling, and a pure B2B customer base.**

## Bottom line
- Cyber Resilience Act: In Scope, Prio 1 — connected sensors and controllers are "products with digital elements," triggering vulnerability handling, ENISA notification, and CE-marking cybersecurity obligations that require dedicated engineering and compliance resourcing.
- Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC: In Scope, Prio 1 — factory-automation controllers fall under essential health and safety conformity-assessment requirements that are currently enforced and will transition to a successor regime by 20 January 2027, making this a live safety-compliance obligation, not a future one.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cyber Resilience Act (EU) 2024/2847 | 1 | **In Scope** | Manufacturers of products with digital elements must report vulnerabilities and cooperate with CSIRT coordinators; ENISA adds publicly known vulnerabilities to the European vulnerability database in agreement with the manufacturer[1], and CSIRTs provide helpdesk support on reporting obligations to manufacturers[1] — a large firm gets no simplification, only the full obligation set. |
| Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC | 1 | **In Scope** | The company is a "manufacturer" under the Directive's own test: any natural or legal person who designs and/or manufactures machinery or partly completed machinery covered by this Directive and is responsible for the conformity of the machinery... with a view to its being placed on the market, under his own name or trademark[2]. Successor Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027 — plan the transition, but 2006/42/EC governs now. |
| Data Act (EU) 2023/2854 | 2 | **In Scope** | As a large manufacturer of connected products, no SME design-obligation relief and no medium-enterprise transitional period apply — it would be overly burdensome on microenterprises and small enterprises to impose further design obligations in relation to connected products[3] is an exemption this company does not qualify for. |
| NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 | 2 | **In Scope** | Manufacture of machinery and equipment is an explicitly listed sector: Manufacture of machinery and equipment n.e.c. — undertakings carrying out any of the economic activities referred to in section C division 28 of NACE Rev. 2[4], and the company's "large" size places it squarely in the important/essential entity tier. |
| Cybersecurity Act (EU) 2019/881 | 3 | **Monitor** | Certification schemes for IoT remain largely voluntary today; hinges on whether the Commission designates a mandatory scheme for industrial IoT components — cybersecurity certification plays an important role in increasing trust and security in ICT products... the digital single market, and in particular the data economy and the IoT, can thrive only if there is general public trust[5]. |

The Cyber Resilience Act is the file to build a resourcing plan around. It is not a distant proposal but an adopted regulation whose obligations attach directly to the manufacturer at the point of vulnerability discovery and market placement, and it explicitly contemplates ongoing regulator interaction rather than a one-off filing: CSIRTs designated as coordinators shall provide helpdesk support in relation to the reporting obligations pursuant to Article 14 to manufacturers[1]. Because the company does not qualify as a micro or small enterprise, it gets none of the simplified pathways built into the Regulation for smaller players, meaning full technical documentation, vulnerability-disclosure processes, and authorised-representative arrangements are all live workstreams now, not contingencies.

## Political landscape & strategic play
The Cyber Resilience Act sits with DG CONNECT and ENISA operationally, with ENISA running the vulnerability database and CSIRT coordination described above — this is the working-level contact point for technical guidance rather than the political leadership. The Machinery file sits with DG GROW and the European Standardisation Organisations (CEN-CENELEC), which are actively drafting the harmonised standards manufacturers need for presumption of conformity: the production of European harmonised standards for IoT, AI-powered advanced robots and autonomous systems is ongoing... to offer a level playing field and a competitive advantage to European manufacturers[6]. These standards bodies, not the Commission directly, are where technical specification battles actually get won.

On the Data Act, the Commission's own stakeholder consultation shows industry consolidating around a "unified framework" position rather than fragmentation: companies obliged to adapt their data systems under the Data Act acknowledged compliance costs but saw the requirements as manageable... they rejected calls to replace the Act with sector-specific rules, favouring a unified framework to avoid regulatory fragmentation[7]. That consultation also flagged the trade-secrets "handbrake" as a live fault line worth watching: several participants warned that manufacturers might overuse the "trade secrets" clause... to restrict data access[7], with calls for clearer guidance.

**Lobbying focus:** the standardisation process for CRA and Machinery Regulation harmonised standards is where this company's technical input has the most leverage — CEN-CENELEC working groups, not direct Commission lobbying, are drafting the presumption-of-conformity standards the company will need by 2027.

**Coalitions:**
- Industrial manufacturers already organized in the Data Act stakeholder consultation around a unified-framework position are a natural door for aligning on trade-secrets guidance and model contract terms.
- No CRA- or Machinery-specific industry coalition is named in the retrieved sources; engagement here runs through standards bodies rather than an existing trade-association bloc.

**Watchlist:**
- 20 January 2027 — Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 becomes applicable, replacing Directive 2006/42/EC; conformity documentation should be Regulation-ready well before this date.
- Ongoing — CEN-CENELEC harmonised standards work for IoT, AI-powered systems and combined products, which will define presumption-of-conformity routes under both CRA and the Machinery Regulation.
- Ongoing — Commission guidance development on the Data Act trade-secrets "handbrake," flagged by stakeholders as a compliance risk area to watch.

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Panel (Regional Logistics & Warehousing Operator)

**No EU digital-regulation regime currently binds this company; the only open questions are whether NIS2 and the Critical Entities Resilience Directive sweep in freight/last-mile logistics as a covered sector.**

## Bottom line

- ACTION: NIS2 cybersecurity obligations hinge on whether last-mile delivery counts as "postal and courier services" under the Directive's scope — confirm classification with the BSI before assuming exemption.
- ACTION: Critical Entities Resilience Directive exposure hinges on whether Germany's KRITIS designation process names this operator as a critical transport-sector entity — confirm designation status, don't assume out.

No RISK or OPPORTUNITY attention bullets apply: the company reports no AI use, no personal data handling, no digital product, and a B2B customer base, so none of the enforcement-heavy or competitor-driven dynamics in the canon (GDPR, DMA, DSA, AI Act) touch this business today.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) | 2 | **Monitor** | Scope for medium-sized entities is automatic once sector fit is established — the Directive applies a size-cap rule whereby entities qualifying as medium-sized enterprises "which operate within the sectors and provide the types of service or carry out the activities covered by this Directive fall within its scope."[1] Company is medium-sized; the open question is whether last-mile delivery qualifies as postal/courier services — confirm with BSI. |
| Critical Entities Resilience Directive (32022L2557) | 3 | **Monitor** | Transport is a listed critical sector, but coverage depends on Member State designation of specific "critical entities," not an automatic size test — confirm whether the German KRITIS process has named this operator. |

NIS2 is the instrument worth the most attention here, even at Monitor status, because its scope trigger is structural rather than discretionary. Unlike the CER Directive, which requires an active Member State designation, NIS2's size-cap rule pulls in medium enterprises automatically once their sector and service type match Annex I or II — the Directive was designed precisely "to eliminate the wide divergences among Member States" that existed under the old NIS Directive by imposing a uniform, non-discretionary criterion[1]. That means the compliance question for this company is not "will the state designate us" but "does our activity fit the sectoral list" — a fact question, not a political one, and one the company can resolve directly with the BSI rather than waiting on a government decision. Germany's national transposition (NIS2UmsuCG) has been delayed relative to the Directive's original 17 October 2024 Member State deadline, which gives the company a real window to clarify classification before enforcement risk becomes live.

## Political landscape & strategic play

In Germany, NIS2 implementation sits with the Federal Ministry of the Interior (BMI) as policy lead and the Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI) as the operational supervisory authority that will issue sector guidance and handle registration once the national transposition law is in force. The BSI is the working-level body to approach for a scope determination — not the Commission, which has already finished its legislative role on this file. On the CER Directive, the same KRITIS regime and BMI/BSI apparatus that runs national critical-infrastructure identification also governs designation, meaning a single relationship covers both open questions.

No retrieved source shows a live legislative fight, floor debate, or organized coalition specifically contesting NIS2's sectoral scope for logistics or courier services, and none names a competitor whose NIS2 or CER posture creates commercial upside for this company. The retrieved political material on the wider digital simplification agenda (Digital Omnibus-style proposals) documents Commission outreach to SMEs through the Enterprise Europe Network but does not tie any specific rollback to this company's sector or a named rival.

**Lobbying focus**: engagement should be scoping, not advocacy — the highest-value action is a direct written scope inquiry to the BSI (or its designated NIS2 registration portal once national transposition completes) requesting a formal classification of freight storage and last-mile delivery against Annex II "postal and courier services." This is a routine administrative-clarification ask well within a medium-sized regional operator's capacity, not an escalation.

**Coalitions**: the retrieved sources name no logistics-sector trade association or complainant group organized specifically around NIS2 or CER scope questions — this is a genuine gap, not an omission; a national logistics or transport association would be the natural venue to build if one becomes relevant.

**Watchlist**:
- Finalization of Germany's NIS2UmsuCG transposition law — determines binding registration deadlines and the sector list actually enforced.
- BSI sector guidance publication on courier/postal service scope — the single document that resolves the NIS2 hinge.
- Germany's KRITIS critical-entity designation cycle for the transport sector — resolves the CER hinge.
- Any Commission Digital Omnibus follow-through on SME simplification — could affect future compliance cost even for currently out-of-scope files like GDPR if the company's data-handling profile changes.

# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: [B2B Project-Management SaaS]

**GDPR is the only live, must-fix obligation today; every other EU digital-file (DMA, DSA, AI Act, Data Act, NIS2, CRA) is out of scope at this size, with cookie-tracking and cross-border pricing practices the two facts worth confirming before year-end.**

## Bottom line

- ACTION: GDPR is Prio 1 — the company processes personal data with no dedicated compliance function, and this is a live, actively enforced regime with no size exemption beyond a bookkeeping derogation.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDPR (EU) 2016/679 | 1 | **In Scope** | Processes personal data as controller/processor; only relief available is that this Regulation includes a derogation for organisations with fewer than 250 employees with regard to record-keeping[1] — everything else (lawful basis, DSRs, breach notice) applies in full. |
| ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC | 2 | **Monitor** | Cookie/tracker consent rules on terminal equipment turn on whether measures are adopted to ensure terminal equipment is constructed in a way that is compatible with the right of users to protect and control the use of their personal data[2] — hinges on whether the marketing site runs non-essential analytics/ad trackers; confirm. |
| Geo-blocking Regulation (EU) 2018/302 | 2 | **Monitor** | Non-discrimination duty applies because consumers and undertakings, in particular microenterprises and SMEs, are often in a similar position... both consumers and undertakings should be protected against discrimination for reasons related to their nationality, place of residence or place of establishment when acting as customers[3] — hinges on whether pricing or contract terms differ by customer country; confirm. |

GDPR is the file that actually bites. It is the only instrument in this table backed by a supervisory infrastructure that is still being actively strengthened rather than merely proposed: the EDPB's cooperation and consistency procedure was just given a dedicated early-resolution mechanism, letting the supervisory authority with which the complaint has been lodged... resolve a complaint concerning cross-border processing... prior to the possible transmission of the complaint to the supervisory authority presumed to be competent to act as lead supervisory authority[4]. That is a sign the enforcement machinery for cross-border SaaS complaints is getting faster, not slower — a two-person startup with EU customers in multiple member states should not assume enforcement friction buys it time. The only structural relief available at this size is administrative (record-keeping), not substantive: lawful-basis documentation, a data processing agreement template for engineering-team customers, and a breach-notification runbook are the concrete gaps to close.

## Political landscape & strategic play

GDPR enforcement runs through the company's lead national Data Protection Authority (determined by main EU establishment) coordinated by the EDPB under the one-stop-shop mechanism, now supplemented by the early-resolution procedure in Regulation (EU) 2025/2518 described above. There is no rapporteur or committee fight here — this is a mature enforcement regime, not a live legislative file, so the working-level contact that matters is the DPA's SME/startup helpdesk, not a Brussels dossier owner.

The one genuinely live legislative track relevant to this company's future is the Commission's SME/SMC relief package amending the AI Act and Data Act, which inserts a formal small mid-cap definition and targeted derogations. The proposal inserts measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on small mid-cap enterprises (SMCs) and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), including start-ups[5]. It matters now only as a watch-item: if the company ever adopts AI features, this is the track that will shape the compliance burden it inherits.

**Lobbying focus**: the highest-value venue at this size is not direct Brussels engagement but the European Enterprise Network, which the Commission already uses to run structured SME consultations — it managed a targeted survey to micro, small, and medium enterprises (SME) referred to as the "SME Panel Consultation" or "Panel"[6] on prior digital-file revisions. A realistic ask is submitting a short position note through a horizontal SME/startup association during the next such consultation window, not engaging the Commission directly.

**Coalitions**:
- SME and SMC associations already organized around Data Act implementation, having strongly urged for a forceful implementation of the rules[7] — the right door for input on data-sharing burden as the company scales.
- Horizontal SME/startup bodies feeding the AI Act SME/SMC relief package (doc SWD(2025)836) — relevant once AI features are added.
- No named competitor or gatekeeper dynamic is documented in the retrieved sources for this company's specific market, so no DMA/DSA-style competitive opening applies here.

**Watchlist**:
- Ongoing negotiation of the AI Act/Data Act SME-SMC relief proposal (COM(2025)0836) — defines SMC status and derogations the company may later benefit from.
- Data Act's lighter cloud-switching regime for SMEs/SMCs, estimated to positively affect 5000 of such companies[7] — relevant once the company is a cloud services customer seeking to switch providers.
- Continued rollout of the EDPB early-resolution procedure under Regulation (EU) 2025/2518 — watch for faster cross-border GDPR complaint handling.
- Any move to reclassify cloud-based SaaS tools under NIS2's Annex I "digital infrastructure" list independent of the current size-cap rule — would change today's Out of Scope call if the size-cap exemption is narrowed.

profiles.briefing:
# Regulatory Intelligence Brief: Consumer AI Symptom-Checker Startup

**GDPR governs day one because of the health-data processing; the AI Act's applicability is the single open question that decides whether this is a light-touch consumer-tech build or a full high-risk conformity programme, and that turns on a medical-device classification call the profile does not yet settle.**

## Bottom line
- GDPR is Prio 1: the app processes health data on a B2C basis under a special-category regime already live and enforced — this is baseline, non-negotiable compliance, not a future obligation.
- AI Act is Prio 1 but Monitor: the classification hinge is whether the symptom-checker is a "safety component" of a medical device or otherwise Annex III high-risk — confirm this before any product or funding decision, because it determines whether conformity assessment, a QMS and a fundamental rights impact assessment are mandatory from the start.

## Compliance exposure

| Instrument | Prio | Verdict | Why / Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDPR (32016R0679) | 1 | **In Scope** | Health data is special-category personal data processed on a consumer-facing basis; the Regulation exists precisely to give "natural persons... control of their own personal data" Natural persons should have control of their own personal data.[1] under a live, enforced regime. |
| AI Act (32024R1689) | 1 | **Monitor** | Hinges on whether the symptom-checker qualifies as a safety component of a medical device (Annex I harmonisation legislation) or an Annex III high-risk use case — confirm with counsel before launch. The Regulation's stated purpose is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights[2], and its scope provisions determine which obligations bite. |
| Product Liability Directive (32024L2853) | 2 | **In Scope** | The Directive treats AI providers as manufacturers: A developer or producer of software, including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council, should be treated as a manufacturer.[3] No-fault liability attaches to the app as software. |
| ePrivacy Directive (32002L0058) | 2 | **In Scope** | Terminal-equipment and communications-privacy safeguards apply regardless of device configuration, since the protection of the personal data and the privacy of the user of publicly available electronic communications services should be independent of the configuration of the various components necessary to provide the service[4] — cookie/consent hygiene on the app is required. |
| Consumer Rights Directive as amended (32024L0825 / 32011L0083) | 2 | **In Scope** | As a digital consumer service, pre-contractual information duties apply; the amending Directive requires that specific information about a product's durability and reparability should be provided for all types of goods before concluding the contract... as regards goods with digital elements, digital content and digital services, consumers should be informed about the period during which free software updates are available.[5] |
| Cyber Resilience Act (32024R2847) | 2 | **Monitor** | Hinges on the same medical-device classification question: if the app is regulated as a medical device it is likely carved out of CRA scope; if not, the app is a "product with digital elements" subject to CRA's cybersecurity-by-design obligations. Confirm classification before treating either regime as settled. |
| EHDS Regulation (32025R0327) | 2 | **Monitor** | Hinges on whether the app is treated as a regulated EHR/health-data-exchange system triggering mandatory digital-health-authority oversight, or a voluntary wellness application outside that regime — EHDS explicitly contemplates Member States should designate relevant digital health authorities for the planning and implementation of standards for access to and transmission of electronic health data and the enforcement of the rights of natural persons and health professionals[6], but the trigger depends on the app's exact data role. |
| Digital Omnibus package (52025PC0836, 52025PC0837, 52026PC0502) | 3 | **Monitor** | Proposed amendments would streamline AI Office supervision and GDPR–AI Act interplay; none are yet adopted law, so nothing to resource now beyond tracking. |

The AI Act carries the brief because its consequence swings the furthest depending on one fact this startup must nail down early. If the symptom-checker functions as a safety component of a medical device, or falls under an Annex III high-risk healthcare use case, the provider obligations are not incremental — they include conformity assessment, technical documentation and post-market monitoring, layered on top of the "specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems" the Regulation lays down specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems[2]. The Commission has signalled it will not let this sit in a legal grey zone: it commits to work with Member States "to ensure the consistent implementation and enforcement of the Artificial Intelligence Act and the relevant consumer protection and product safety laws" The Commission will work closely with Member States to ensure the consistent implementation and enforcement of the Artificial Intelligence Act and the relevant consumer protection and product safety laws.[7], and reviews the prohibited-practices list annually The list of prohibited AI practices under the Artificial Intelligence Act will be reviewed annually and updated if new problems are identified.[7] — a live, moving compliance target, not a static one this startup can set-and-forget after launch.

## Political landscape & strategic play

Enforcement of AI systems tied to Union harmonisation legislation — the medical-device route relevant here — stays with sectoral authorities even as the AI Office's remit expands: the Commission's own proposal confirms that sectoral authorities continue to remain responsible for the supervision of AI systems related to products covered by that Union harmonisation legislation, Article 75(1) Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 should be modified to bring all AI systems based on general-purpose AI models developed by the same provider within the scope of the AI Office's supervision.[8] For a French-market health app, that means the national medical-devices competent authority and CNIL (data protection) are the working-level bodies to watch, not the Brussels-level AI Office alone. On the health-data side, EHDS designates national digital health authorities as the operational contact point, and these bodies are expected to coordinate with GDPR supervisory authorities and the future AI Board When carrying out their tasks, digital health authorities should cooperate in particular with the supervisory authorities established pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and supervisory bodies established pursuant to Regulation (EU) No 910/2014.[6]

**Lobbying focus**: the highest-value engagement for a micro startup is not confrontation but clarification — submitting evidence to the Commission's consumer-protection and AI enforcement work described in its 2025 Communication, which explicitly signals openness to sector input on AI-consumer interaction transparency it is crucial that the consumer protection framework keeps pace with technological developments and that consumers have transparent information when they interact with AI (e.g. when using AI powered customer service support or seeking information and advice from AI assistants)[7]. A short submission on how symptom-checker transparency should be operationalised is a realistic, scaled ask.

**Coalitions**: the retrieved sources name no trade association or peer-company coalition organized specifically around consumer AI health apps — this is a genuine gap, not an omission; a health-tech or digital-SME association would need to be identified independently.

**Watchlist**:
- Ongoing co-decision on the Digital Omnibus proposals (52025PC0836, 52025PC0837, 52026PC0502) reshaping AI Office/GDPR interplay — no fixed date in the retrieved texts, but adoption would directly change this startup's governance burden.
- Annual review of the AI Act's prohibited-practices list The list of prohibited AI practices under the Artificial Intelligence Act will be reviewed annually and updated if new problems are identified.[7] — recurring compliance-calendar item.
- EHDS digital health authority designations across Member States, which will clarify whether wellness/symptom apps face mandatory oversight Digital health authorities already exist in most of the Member States and they deal with EHRs, interoperability, security or standardisation.[6]
